## KI#184.3 - (Fixed/Improved) Base AdvCiv/K-Mod ordinary production reevaluation can repeatedly park heavily invested launch-required spaceship components

Screenshots/files for this issue: [google drive folder link](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1HjhMD3HN8nk1usorT9qdwxdhi6i8ckeS?usp=sharing).

A late-game SASGameRecord review first exposed this through a Rome/Khmer space race. In the practical 6411 record `SASGameRecord_20260907T142638Z_new1.log`, Rome completed Apollo on turn 283 and established a large space-production lead, but repeatedly parked already-invested Engines and Docking Bays while reacting to ordinary city production priorities. The motivating examples included an Engine in Mediolanum, an Engine in Cumae with roughly 1064/1880 production, a Docking Bay in Antium with 651/1880 production, and later another Docking Bay attempt in Nicaea. Rome ultimately completed 15 of the 16 maximum spaceship parts but still lacked the mandatory Docking Bay when Khmer won on turn 406. The important failure was therefore not ignorance of the spaceship requirement: Rome started the required part multiple times, but local city production reevaluation repeatedly overrode the empire's near-term launch bottleneck.

Source investigation showed that the underlying continuity gap is inherited rather than introduced by AdvCiv-SAS. A direct local comparison against the user's archived `AdvCiv-1.14.zip` confirms that Base AdvCiv 1.14 `CvCityAI::AI_chooseProduction` contains continuity exceptions for food-production units, items with at most a few turns remaining, an undefended city's combat unit and sufficiently progressed limited buildings, but no corresponding protection for an invested spaceship project before the ordinary queue is cleared and production is selected again. The same Base AdvCiv source labels `AI_chooseProduction` as heavily edited by K-Mod and `AI_bestProject` as significantly modified for K-Mod; that inherited project scheduler assigns SPACE3 project fit mainly from production rank and full project thresholds and does not by itself preserve the city that already owns most of a launch-critical component. SAS production changes can alter how often the inherited weakness becomes visible, but the demonstrated continuity gap is present in Base AdvCiv 1.14 and is not an SAS regression.

A dedicated `SAS_BBAI_SPACE_PRODUCTION_LOG_LEVEL` category was added because SASGameRecord could identify the strategic outcome and production switches but could not explain the city-level project valuation and branch that displaced them. Level 2 records invested spaceship reevaluation/release/final-target transitions and selected projects; level 3 additionally records every spaceship candidate's legality, production-rank/fit decision and the space-specific project value before and after victory-stage, area-war and production-capacity adjustments. This diagnostic has no RNG calls and is intended to remain disabled by default after testing.

Two current-source unfixed diagnostic replays reproduced the same class of failure independently. In `BBAI_20260912T193450Z_load1.log`, Ethiopia won on turn 389 while Rome ended with 14/16 spaceship parts, missing the Stasis Chamber and Docking Bay. In `BBAI_20260912T194918Z_load1.log`, Ethiopia won on turn 426 while Rome ended with 15/16, again missing only the Docking Bay. The second run produced a particularly clear smoking gun: on turn 412 Rome had 1469/1880 production (78%) in its sole missing Docking Bay, only 5 turns remaining, SPACE4 active and no immediate city danger, yet ordinary `AI_chooseProduction` reevaluation released it for a 1-turn Work Boat. At the same decision point the inherited production-rank fit could rate a different Roman city with zero Docking Bay investment as the preferred project city, while the 78%-complete city was treated as a poor fit. This established that the problem was not merely a low generic project value during war; substantial sunk project progress could be discarded by the interaction of ordinary production reevaluation and cross-city project fit.

The first targeted prototype therefore added a deliberately narrow continuity rule rather than a global spaceship scheduler. During SPACE4, a safe AI city kept an already-invested spaceship component when that project was still below its `VictoryMinThreshold` and had at most 20 Normal-speed-equivalent project turns remaining, scaled by `CreatePercent`. Optional extra pieces remained fully reevaluable and immediate city danger still overrode continuity. The purpose was to protect the exact near-term launch bottleneck without permanently locking obviously poor 40-80-turn assignments.

Two full replays with that prototype showed a large directional improvement, although the exact winner remains stochastic after the behavior change. In `BBAI_20260912T202036Z_load1.log`, Rome's launch-critical projects repeatedly hit the continuity rule; Rome launched on turn 350 and won the Space Race on turn 362. In `BBAI_20260912T202902Z_load2.log`, Ethiopia instead launched and won on turn 364, while Rome had already reached 15/16 and was actively rebuilding its last missing Stasis Chamber. These outcomes should not be read as "continuity guarantees Rome wins": autoplay histories diverge once production choices change. They do show that both prototype runs produced much earlier and more decisive space-race execution than the two immediately preceding unfixed replays that ended on turns 389 and 426.

The dedicated logging also exposed two flaws in that first prototype before it was considered commit-ready. First, Rome simultaneously protected two Engines in the first fixed replay even though the minimum launch requirement needs only one Engine: both cities saw `minimumRequired=1` and `currentCount=0`, so the local continuity check did not account for another city already producing the same minimum component. Protecting every concurrent copy could turn an optional second component into an unintended sticky project. Second, the second fixed replay exposed a safe Roman Stasis Chamber in Thessalonica at 858/1880 production (45%) and 22 turns remaining on turn 339. Rome was at SPACE3 but not yet SPACE4, so the prototype did not apply; the city released the Stasis Chamber for 4-turn Public Transportation and Rome later finished the game one Stasis Chamber short. This is strong direct evidence that SPACE4/20 turns was too narrow even though the basic continuity idea was useful.

The current follow-up candidate therefore starts continuity at SPACE3, matching the stage where inherited K-Mod already begins its production-rank spaceship scheduling, and raises the default tunable gate to 25 Normal-speed-equivalent project turns. It also ranks concurrently produced eligible copies of the same minimum-required component by fewer remaining turns, then greater stored production, then stable player/city identity, and protects only as many copies as the team's still-missing `VictoryMinThreshold` actually requires. A lower-ranked concurrent duplicate logs `SPACE_PRODUCTION_CONTINUITY_SKIP ... reason=duplicate_beyond_minimum` and remains normally reevaluable. This preserves the useful near-launch continuity while avoiding the first prototype's duplicate-Engine overprotection.

Two further full replays with the SPACE3+/25-turn/minimum-copy-ranked refinement validated the duplicate protection but also separated game-result variance from the local continuity mechanism. In `BBAI_20260912T213146Z_load1.log`, the duplicate filter fired repeatedly (20 `duplicate_beyond_minimum` rows overall); for example, on turn 325 Nicaea's second Roman Engine at 76/1880 and 22 turns was left reevaluable while Thessalonica's better Engine at 185/1880 and 16 turns received continuity and then stayed protected through completion. Rome nevertheless did not win that game because it was eventually eliminated; Ethiopia launched a complete 16-part ship and won on turn 407. In `BBAI_20260912T214201Z_load2.log`, the duplicate filter fired 11 more times and Thessalonica's minimum Engine was kept continuously from 51%/20 turns through 99%/1 turn. Ethiopia still launched first on turn 380 and won on turn 387. Rome was alive and had completed the Cockpit, Life Support, Docking Bay, one Engine, all five Casings and four Thrusters; its remaining launch blocker was the Stasis Chamber, which Nicaea was actively building at 930/1880 with 15 turns remaining when the game ended. Julius Caesar therefore not winning these refined runs is not evidence that continuity failed: one Rome was conquered, while the other was simply beaten to launch/arrival by a faster rival.

The second refined replay did, however, expose one narrower remaining form of the same inherited churn just outside the 25-turn gate. Minoan repeatedly released Rome's still-mandatory Stasis Chamber while safe and at SPACE3: 515/1880 (27%, 43 turns) on turn 341, 579/1880 (30%, 41 turns) on turn 343, 611/1880 (32%, 34 turns) on turn 344, 835/1880 (44%, 33 turns) on turn 350 and 933/1880 (49%, 32 turns) on turn 366. The turn-350 reevaluation switched that 44%-complete mandatory Stasis to an optional Thruster; the turn-366 reevaluation parked the 49%-complete Stasis for a 2-turn Jail. This is the same strategic defect as the original five-turn Docking Bay case, but it also shows why simply raising the universal turn gate is undesirable: a fresh poor 30-40-turn project should still be free to relocate.

The final rule therefore keeps the evidence-backed 25-turn near-term gate and adds a separate heavier-investment fallback: by default, a minimum-required component at least 40% complete can also receive continuity when no more than 40 Normal-speed-equivalent project turns remain. Both turn gates scale by `CreatePercent`. Concurrent eligible copies still use the validated minimum-copy ranking, and immediate city danger still overrides continuity. This two-stage rule is intentionally narrower than a global spaceship scheduler: it protects clearly meaningful sunk launch progress without making every fresh 30-40-turn project sticky.

Two final full replays with this rule confirmed the local objective and, importantly, again showed why the exact winner is not the acceptance criterion. In `BBAI_20260912T221123Z_load1.log` / `SASGameRecord_20260912T221123Z_load1.log`, Ethiopia launched on turn 351 and Rome launched on turn 357; Ethiopia simply arrived first and won on turn 363. In `BBAI_20260912T221928Z_load2.log` / `SASGameRecord_20260912T221928Z_load2.log`, Rome launched on turn 347, Ethiopia launched on turn 351, and Rome arrived first and won on turn 359. Rome therefore completed and launched its minimum spaceship in both independent final replays, in contrast to the two unfixed diagnostic runs that ended with Rome still missing launch-required parts. The duplicate guard continued to behave as intended, with 18 and 11 `duplicate_beyond_minimum` decisions respectively; lower-ranked optional copies remained free to reevaluate while the best still-needed copy received continuity. No safe, invested minimum component inside either active continuity gate was observed being parked for unrelated production. One Roman Docking Bay at 386/1880 and 20 turns was deliberately released on turn 330 in the first run because that city had `danger=1`, confirming that immediate local danger still overrides the optimization. The heavier-investment fallback itself did not need to fire in these two particular trajectories because their protected launch-critical components were already inside the 25-turn near-term gate; its bounded 40%/40-turn fallback remains justified by the immediately preceding replay that directly reproduced the 44%-49%, 32-33-turn Stasis churn.

The investigation is also a good example of the intended division between SASGameRecord and focused BBAI diagnostics: broad game-record screening found the strategic failure across complete autoplays, then the dedicated BBAI space-production category narrowed it to an inherited city-production continuity/fit mechanism, proved the original failure at city-decision granularity, and exposed edge cases in successive proposed fixes. `SAS_BBAI_SPACE_PRODUCTION_LOG_LEVEL` remains available for future targeted investigation but is disabled by default.

Fixed/improved with the help of ChatGPT-5.6-Sol thanks.

## KI#185 - (Fixed/Improved) Base AdvCiv issue: post-capital AI Settlers could ignore promising fogged nearby city-site alternatives and then follow stale cached targets after scouting

Screenshots/files for this issue: [google drive folder link](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1-RaBTEQYMlgIDXpHRokuzQBP-UDYx9Ay?usp=sharing).

This is a follow-up to the save-file 450 uMgungundlovu investigation from KI#178. KI#178 fixed a major bonus-valuation problem: the old broad `AI_bonusVal` path could make Elephants massively outscore Crab for settlement, pushing Shaka toward weaker `(18,40)` instead of the stronger nearby `(17,40)` site. Later BBAI retesting showed a separate remaining movement / information problem: even after bonus valuation was improved, history could change enough that `(17,40)` still looked slightly worse only because more of its BFC was fogged, while `(18,40)` had more known plots.

This is not the same system as first-city roaming in KI#43 / KI#173. First-city scouting happens before the capital exists and uses a bounded capital-search routine. This issue is for post-capital `CvUnitAI::AI_found`, where the AI normally follows cached city-site targets. By then, most nearby land is usually known, so we do not want broad roaming; the useful case is narrow: a Settler is already near a selected site, and an adjacent site has a stronger average known value per revealed BFC plot while still having more unrevealed plots.

In `BBAI_20260715T092145Z_load1.log`, the first half of the new logic worked: Zulu repeatedly chose `PUSH_SCOUT_PROMISING_FOGGED_SITE` toward `(17,40)`:

```text
Settler promising-fogged-site candidate 17,40 selectedValue=3064 value=2959 selectedRevealedBFC=19 revealedBFC=17 selectedUnrevealedBFC=1 unrevealedBFC=3 selectedAvgX100=16126 avgX100=17405 selectedPathTurns=3 pathTurns=3
SETTLER_MISSION_DECISION turn=36 player=7 Zulu Empire action=PUSH_SCOUT_PROMISING_FOGGED_SITE reason=PROMISING_FOGGED_NEAR_SITE ... target=(17,40) ... targetFoundValue=2959 pathTurns=3
```

However, that revealed a second stale-target issue. The Settler reached `(17,40)`, fully revealed it, and the direct found-value comparison now showed it was better than `(18,40)`, but the cached city-site target remained `(18,40)` and the Settler still walked back to found there:

```text
Settler promising-fogged-site candidate 17,40 selectedValue=3993 value=4099 selectedRevealedBFC=20 revealedBFC=20 selectedUnrevealedBFC=0 unrevealedBFC=0 selectedAvgX100=19965 avgX100=20495 selectedPathTurns=1 pathTurns=1
SETTLER_MISSION_DECISION turn=40 player=7 Zulu Empire action=PUSH_MOVE_TO_FOUND ... x=17 y=40 target=(18,40) ... targetFoundValue=3993 pathTurns=1
Shaka is about to found a city at (18,40); turn 40
Best site adjacent to (18,40): selected=3993 adjacent=4099 delta=+106 (17,40)
```

The final fix therefore has two parts:

- post-capital Settlers can make a short exploratory move to an adjacent promising fogged site when its known average value is strong enough and it has enough additional unrevealed BFC plots;
- after such scouting or any similar movement, if the Settler is already standing on a foundable plot that direct replacement scoring now says is better than the cached selected target, it founds there instead of walking away to the stale target.

The debugging path matters because the code looks more specific than a simple adjacent-tile scan:

- first attempt: using adjacent plots' cached `getFoundValue` made `(17,40)` log as `value=0`, because adjacent replacement candidates are not necessarily entries in the current cached city-site list;
- second attempt: switching to a direct evaluator still logged `value=0`, because the evaluator treated `(17,40)` as an extra tentative city overlapping the selected `(18,40)` site;
- third attempt: matching the found-value logger's replacement-site mode with `setDebug(true)` made `(17,40)` score correctly and triggered the scout move;
- final missing piece: once the group reached `(17,40)`, the normal cached target could still remain `(18,40)`, so a current-plot replacement check was needed before moving away.

Implementation details:

- candidate scoring uses a direct `CitySiteEvaluator` pass, not cached `getFoundValue`, because adjacent alternatives may not be in the current city-site list and can otherwise read as `0`;
- the evaluator uses `setDebug(true)` for these comparisons, matching the found-value logger's adjacent-site mode, so the alternative is treated as a replacement for the selected site rather than an extra tentative city overlapping it;
- the exploratory move uses `MISSIONAI_EXPLORE`, not `MISSIONAI_FOUND`, so `AI_foundFollow` does not blindly found after one move without recalculating.

Retesting in `BBAI_20260715T092627Z_load1.log` / `SASGameRecord_20260715T092627Z_load1.log` confirmed the intended result:

```text
SETTLER_MISSION_DECISION turn=40 player=7 Zulu Empire action=FOUND_CURRENT_SITE_BETTER_THAN_SELECTED_TARGET reason=CURRENT_SITE_NOW_BETTER ... x=17 y=40 target=(17,40) ... targetFoundValue=4099 pathTurns=0
Shaka is about to found a city at (17,40); turn 40
Selected site breakdown value=4099 ... bonuses=2077(nonYield=1302,bonusImprovementYields=775) ...
Best site adjacent to (17,40): selected=4099 adjacent=3993 delta=-106 (18,40)
GAME_RECORD_ACTION turn=40 type=CITY_BUILT player=7 cityId=16385 city="uMgungundlovu" x=17 y=40 pop=1
```

This founded uMgungundlovu at `(17,40)` with Crab/Rice/Camel and a better food profile, instead of the stale `(18,40)` Elephants/Rice/Camel site. Follow-up testing with the extra-path limit raised to 3 in `BBAI_20260715T100351Z_load1.log` / `SASGameRecord_20260715T100351Z_load1.log` preserved the same `(17,40)` result, showed no obvious Settler parking by turn 101, and produced only three actual promising-fog scout chains in the run. This supports default 3 as local enough while still allowing more than one-tile-only correction attempts.

This should make post-capital Settlers less brittle around small fog differences without turning them into broad wandering scouts.

Fixed/improved with the help of GPT-5.5 (on ChatGPT Codex) thanks.

## KI#186 - (Fixed/Improved) Base AdvCiv `AI_isAwfulSite` could cause economically wasteful captured-city raze/resettle cycles and destroy valuable population and buildings

Screenshots/files for this issue: [google drive folder link](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1bbizfK11MiZcM8TDvvlbzCe9dq5jx-4a?usp=sharing).

Base AdvCiv used `CvPlayerAI::AI_isAwfulSite` as an absolute veto before its broader captured-city valuation. The function also participated in AI city-trade denial. It tried to decide whether a city was located where no city probably belonged by counting broadly decent natural plots, visible bonuses, and partial coastal value, while excluding impassable, overlapping, or third-party-culture plots. Population and era could protect some cities, but the function remained a separate, crude city-site evaluator rather than sharing the more complete AdvCiv-SAS Settler-site logic.

Diagnostic BBAI logging exposed a stark failure at `(38,50)`. One AI razed Ur there; Tours was then founded on the exact tile and razed; HRE founded Augsburg on the exact tile only four turns later and eventually razed it too. The repeated resettlement proved that the site was not actually useless to the AI. The absolute `AI_isAwfulSite` result was destroying cities that the expansion logic still wanted.

This was highly economically inefficient. Each raze discarded accumulated population, buildings, culture, and city development. Resettling then consumed another Settler and forced the replacement city to regrow and rebuild. Repeated capture and defense also committed military units to the same location without securing durable value. Conversely, keeping a genuinely faraway city can be similarly inefficient: our units can be exhausted defending an isolated outpost, then a nearer rival can capture the already-developed city without paying for its own Settler or initial growth. The correct question is therefore not simply whether the terrain looks "awful", but whether acquiring the city is likely to benefit the recipient long-term.

Ideally, the intrinsic-site part would ask the same canonical evaluator that decides whether a Settler wants to found on the plot. That would prevent one subsystem from destroying a city as a bad site while another soon spends a Settler to rebuild on the exact tile. We did not directly call the full `AI_foundValue` / `CitySiteEvaluator` path because it is designed for prospective unoccupied city sites and the surrounding founding system also relies on cached candidate sites and Settler-specific selection. Base AdvCiv's own `AI_isAwfulSite` comment already noted that `AI_foundValue` is difficult to use on a plot containing an actual city. Reusing it safely here would require an explicit existing-city/replacement mode with carefully defined ownership and overlap behavior, which is a broader refactor than this fix.

Even a safe founding score would cover only intrinsic site desirability, not the whole acquisition decision. A captured or traded city already has population, buildings, culture, maintenance, strategic position, and defensive exposure; a very good founding site can still be a poor acquisition if it is too far away to hold. The replacement therefore reuses the same stable AdvCiv-SAS plot-level potential-yield and food-pressure helpers for intrinsic quality, while leaving developed-city value to the normal conquest / `AI_cityTradeVal` logic and handling sustainable same-area distance separately. This reduces contradictory raze-versus-settle judgments without pretending that "worth founding" and "worth acquiring long-term" are identical questions.

The old function has been disabled and retained in comments for Base AdvCiv reference. Its active conquest and city-trade uses were replaced by the positive `CvPlayerAI::AI_isSASCityLikelyToBenefitUsLongTerm` predicate:

- Intrinsic quality uses the shared AdvCiv-SAS potential-yield and low-food-environment helpers instead of repeating a separate terrain-count formula.
- A site fails intrinsic quality only when it exceeds both the tunable very-bad-BFC-plot limit and the tunable net-low-food limit. This lets strong food sources such as Flood Plains and improved bonuses support otherwise weak plots.
- On the same land area, a city beyond the tunable distance from the recipient's nearest city fails regardless of intrinsic quality. This represents the defensive and economic risk of an isolated developed outpost. If the recipient has no city on that land area, this specific distance gate does not decide the result; broader colony and captured-city logic still applies.
- Overlap, culture pressure, feature health, bonuses, and food-surplus/deficit plot counts remain logged for evidence, but culture pressure and overlap are not hard intrinsic blockers.
- The conquest caller still excludes Barbarians, holy cities, and cities the player previously owned before running this evaluation. Normal captured-city valuation still decides among cities that pass. The city-trade path then continues to `AI_cityTradeVal` for the developed city's broader acquisition value. The active-World-Wonder follow-up is documented separately in KI#186.2.

The thresholds are XML-tunable through `SAS_AI_CITY_LONG_TERM_MAX_VERY_BAD_BFC_PLOTS`, `SAS_AI_CITY_LONG_TERM_MAX_LOW_FOOD_SCORE`, and `SAS_AI_CITY_LONG_TERM_MAX_NEAREST_OWN_CITY_DISTANCE_SAME_AREA`; KI#186.2 covers the separate World-Wonder option. `RAZE_LONG_TERM_CITY_EVAL` logs the raw and protected intrinsic results plus the distance result, and `RAZE_FORCED_REASON reason=SAS_UNLIKELY_LONG_TERM_BENEFIT` identifies conquests where this replacement actually forced the raze. This complements KI#64's earlier early-game remote-city protection: KI#64 addresses especially costly early expansion, while this predicate evaluates long-term site quality and same-area distance at any era, subject to the conquest exclusions.

The first therapeutic retest in `BBAI_20260715T161347Z_load1.log` and `SASGameRecord_20260715T161347Z_load1.log` fixed the exact `(38,50)` failure. HRE captured Ur at turn 130 with population 3. The new evaluation reported `veryBadPlots=8`, `lowFoodScore=23`, and `intrinsicSiteLikelyToBenefit=1`: eight very bad plots were permitted by the configured maximum, so the site was not rejected merely because its low-food score exceeded the other limit. HRE kept Ur. It subsequently reached population 13, built `BUILDING_CORPORATION_5`, generated a Great Engineer, and still had population 11 at turn 300. This confirmed that the formerly razed site could produce durable value when allowed to grow.

The same run's new distance razes also looked strategically justified:

- Bulgar was razed at same-area distance 15 on turn 103; the existing early-remote rules independently selected it too, and nobody resettled nearby.
- Yue-Chi was razed at same-area distance 17 on turn 180, and nobody founded within three plots through turn 300.
- Orleans was razed at same-area distance 10 on turn 257 despite population 13, but France had lost it to Maya on turn 254 and Maya lost it to Persia only three turns later. Persia owned only the city-center plot, all 20 surrounding plots had third-party culture, and nobody founded within three plots during the remaining 43 turns. The history supported the conclusion that this developed city was exposed and unlikely to provide Persia durable value.

The next run in `BBAI_20260715T195321Z_load1.log` and `SASGameRecord_20260715T195321Z_load1.log` reinforced the intrinsic-versus-distance split. Egypt kept Lakamha at same-area distance 4, grew it from population 7 to 17, built the Forbidden Palace and a spaceship part, and generated a Great Person; distant England later razed it at distance 13. Japan kept Giza at distance 4, while England later razed it at distance 11 after repeated conquests. Korea razed population-18 Walata at distance 22. Conversely, Egypt kept isolated Scythian because it had no existing Egyptian city on that land area; it grew from population 5 to 7, confirming that the same-area gate does not automatically reject an overseas foothold.

No city in either retest failed intrinsic quality alone. Ur was the closest boundary case, and its later success supports keeping the strict combined threshold rather than reviving a broad terrain veto. Further autoplay logs can still refine the XML values, but the observed repeated raze/resettle waste was fixed and the new forced razes did not recreate it.

Fixed/improved with the help of GPT-5.6-Sol (on ChatGPT Codex) thanks.

## KI#186.2 - (Fixed/Improved) Base AdvCiv active-World-Wonder exemption could make the AI retain remote captured cities, exhaust defenders, and return the preserved Wonder to a nearer rival

Screenshots/files for this issue: [google drive folder link](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1tiU9J53BJqL92RBCBZ0oIv9uM4zyA6Tv?usp=sharing).

This exemption came from Base AdvCiv, not AdvCiv-SAS. Its conquest condition, introduced under `advc.122` and later kept under `advc.ctr`, required `!kCity.hasActiveWorldWonder() && AI_isAwfulSite(kCity, true)` before the awful-site gate could force a raze. It was authored by f1rpo in Base AdvCiv history years before the AdvCiv-SAS changes. The KI#186 replacement for `AI_isAwfulSite` initially preserved that inherited active-World-Wonder exemption for the new long-term city evaluation. This could make the Wonder dominate the decision even when the captured city was too far away to defend durably. Briefly keeping the Wonder was not useful if a nearer rival could recapture the developed city after our army had been weakened there.

BBAI testing in `BBAI_20260715T195321Z_load1.log` / `SASGameRecord_20260715T195321Z_load1.log` reproduced that failure with England's capture of population-18 Elephantine at distance 15. Its active Eiffel Tower prevented the long-term evaluation. England committed 15 defenders there by turn 230; Egypt killed at least 7 logged English defenders on the city plot and recaptured Elephantine on turn 233, only 6 turns after England had taken it. England gained no durable city or Wonder benefit and instead exhausted units to preserve the Eiffel Tower briefly for nearby Egypt.

The conquest logic now has the default-enabled `SAS_AI_CITY_LONG_TERM_DISTANCE_OVERRIDE_ACTIVE_WORLD_WONDER_ENABLE`. An active World Wonder still protects the city's intrinsic site quality, but it no longer bypasses excessive same-area distance. This keeps a nearby Wonder city eligible for normal captured-city valuation while allowing a truly remote one to be razed, permanently denying the Wonder instead of donating it back after a costly defense. Barbarian, holy-city, and previously-owned-city exclusions remain unchanged.

Save-file 453 provided the direct confirmation in `BBAI_20260716T082233Z_new1.log` / `SASGameRecord_20260716T082233Z_new1.log`. Inca captured population-17 Madrid with an active Statue of Zeus at same-area distance 13. The log reported `intrinsicSiteProtectedByActiveWorldWonder=1`, `distanceOverrideActiveWorldWonder=1`, `sameAreaDistanceLikelyToBenefit=0`, and `RAZE_DECISION ... action=RAZE`. The active Wonder therefore protected intrinsic quality exactly as intended but did not override the unsustainable distance result.

The same save also tested whether the distance limit should be increased from 8 to 9. Population-17 Cordoba at distance 9 and `closeness=16` initially looked like an attractive bridgehead for conquering the nearby Spanish cities, so 9 seemed plausible. The limit-9 A/B retest in `BBAI_20260716T083454Z_load1.log` / `SASGameRecord_20260716T083454Z_load1.log` showed the opposite. Inca kept Cordoba with normal `finalValue=-89`; the Ottomans captured it immediately and killed 2 Incan Robotic Infantry. Inca recaptured it on turn 247, but the Ottomans captured it again on turn 248 and killed 5 Robotic Tanks, 2 more Robotic Infantry, and 1 Gunship. They then transferred the still-developed city back to Spain. Inca lost 10 advanced units defending and recapturing the apparent bridgehead without securing it, reproducing the exact remote-city trap that the distance gate is meant to prevent.

The default distance limit therefore remains 8. It should not be raised merely because a distance-9 city looks valuable or could theoretically anchor further conquest: the slightly larger allowance was enough to split a powerful army around an exposed capture and give the developed city back to a nearer rival. The limit remains XML-tunable for other maps and rulesets, but the tested default favors durable military concentration over speculative bridgeheads.

Fixed/improved with the help of GPT-5.6-Sol (on ChatGPT Codex) thanks.

## KI#186.3 - (Fixed) AdvCiv-SAS regression: captured-city force-raze safeguards could pre-empt Base AdvCiv's Domination keep rule

Screenshots/files for this issue: [google drive folder link](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1WzJN7ZnrUzO1wtKtZ_VGvDp70Oem2lmR?usp=sharing).

This is a follow-up to KI#186 and KI#186.2, but the Domination behavior itself is not a new SAS strategy. Base AdvCiv already had a specific `AI_atVictoryStage(AI_VICTORY_DOMINATION3) && AI_isPrimaryArea(...)` conquest rule telling the AI not to raze such a city. During later AdvCiv-SAS razing work, the old broad `!bCultureVictory` keep-return was removed so awkward conquests could reach normal raze valuation, while the specific Domination keep was retained farther down. KI#186/KI#186.2 then added stronger long-term and distance force-raze safeguards before that inherited block. If one of those earlier gates set `bRaze`, control never reached the later Domination keep. This was therefore an AdvCiv-SAS ordering regression: new safeguards could pre-empt an inherited no-raze priority that was still meant to survive.

The clearest baseline was `BBAI_20260903T055042Z_load3.log` / `SASGameRecord_20260903T055042Z_load3.log`. Isabella kept every conquest through turn 366, then first razed Giza on turn 368 because its same-area distance was 9 against the tested default limit of 8. From turns 389 through 421 she razed 10 consecutive captures: Smolensk, Vladivostok, Dur-Kurigalzu, Yakutsk, Moscow, Rostov, Vilcabamba, Yaroslavl', St. Petersburg, and Coventry. Several were substantial developed cities, including population-14 Dur-Kurigalzu, population-12 Moscow, and population-13 Coventry. Across Isabella's 12 late-game AI razes in this phase, every `RAZE_LONG_TERM_CITY_EVAL` had `rawIntrinsicSiteLikelyToBenefit=1`; they failed only the same-area distance gate. The first distance miss could also make later captures remain farther from the nearest owned city because the razed city never became a new territorial anchor.

| Turn | City | Pop. | Same-area distance | Result |
| ---: | --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| 366 | Nottingham | 10 | 4 | KEEP - Domination |
| **368** | **Giza** | **4** | **9 > 8** | **RAZE** |
| 374 | London | 15 | 4 | KEEP - Domination |
| **389** | **Smolensk** | **1** | **9 > 8** | **RAZE** |
| **400** | **Dur-Kurigalzu** | **14** | **9 > 8** | **RAZE** |
| **405** | **Moscow** | **12** | **16 > 8** | **RAZE** |
| **421** | **Coventry** | **13** | **12 > 8** | **RAZE** |
| 430 | Byblos | 9 | 8 | KEEP - Domination |

The fix is deliberately simpler than the temporary test implementation. Base AdvCiv's explicit Domination3+ primary-area no-raze reason is now hoisted before the SAS long-term, early-remote, and normal raze paths. The now-redundant later copy is removed, as is the temporary XML switch that had been useful for A/B testing. The retained BBAI reason is `DOMINATION3_PRIMARY_AREA_KEEP`. The hoisted condition also preserves AdvCiv's surrounding `!bCultureVictory` exception: if the captured city is part of the inherited near-Cultural-victory danger context, Domination does not auto-keep it merely because the immediate power/local-strength test has not already forced a raze. This restores the inherited priority and exception rather than adding a separate competing Domination rule.

The primary-area restriction is also intentionally retained for now. It comes from Base AdvCiv, and `AI_VICTORY_DOMINATION3` is not synonymous with being one city or one island away from victory: `AI_calculateDominationVictoryStage` can enter stage 3 once the weaker of current land/population progress exceeds `62 - civPlayersEverAlive` percent of the Domination requirement. Removing `AI_isPrimaryArea` at stage 3 would therefore make remote island captures unconditionally untouchable much earlier than a true near-win state, risking the same exposed-bridgehead problem that KI#186.2's distance-8 test fixed. If an any-area endgame rule is later desirable, it should be based on actual closeness to the current Domination land/population thresholds rather than broadening Domination3 blindly.

A full-game A/B retest from the same Pangaea setup and recorded initial RNG state (`mapRandState=814994169`, `syncRandState=1943600988`) strongly supported restoring the inherited priority. In the fixed `BBAI_20260903T064449Z_load2.log` / `SASGameRecord_20260903T064449Z_load2.log`, Ramesses II became the largest practical beneficiary: after the keep path became active he retained 16 primary-area conquests from turn 347 through turn 454 and won Domination on turn 457 at 47.03% land / 53.72% population against 47% / 48% requirements. In the baseline history from the same initial state, Ramesses instead eventually won by Space on turn 464. The diverged histories do not prove that each individual kept city caused the different winner, but they confirm that allowing the inherited Domination keep to run before SAS force-raze gates can convert late military success into the victory the AI is already pursuing.

The design distinction remains important: globally raising the normal distance tolerance is naive. Save-file 453 already showed that increasing 8 to 9 made Inca keep population-17 Cordoba, lose 10 advanced units defending/recapturing the exposed bridgehead, and lose the city anyway. The fix therefore leaves the tested distance/food safeguards unchanged during ordinary conquest and only restores the inherited Domination3+ primary-area veto ahead of them.

Update: A later same-map sanity check (`SASGameRecord_20260903T120258Z_load1.log`) was useful because the game visually looked as if the old regression had returned: Isabella was the dominant late empire and there were many fresh city ruins around the front. The detailed record showed the opposite. Isabella (player 13) had conquered 28 cities by turn 429 and recorded only one raze, population-1 Vitcos on turn 359, which was `AUTO_RAZE` rather than an `AI_conquerCity` choice. The serial late razers were mainly Gandhi (14 recorded razes) and Ramesses II (10).

Several conspicuous ruins had also been created by Isabella's enemies after taking her cities, so map appearance alone was misleading. By turn 429 Isabella was rank 1 with score 4263 and power 5731, had reached Domination4, and was still keeping her normal conquests; she was also simultaneously at war with multiple teams and had lost substantial cities earlier in the same front. This supported the hoisted Domination rule rather than indicating that it had failed.

The same record also argued against broadening the keep veto merely because an AI is the strongest or among the strongest. Ramesses was the highest-power player around turns 310-330 (power 4796 / 4522 / 4878), but remained only at Domination2 and was fighting five teams. During that phase he razed Mari, Shushan, Oxford, Santiago, Argos, and Athens at nearest-own-city distances from 21 through 34 plots. Making military rank or raw power override the normal long-term/distance safeguards would therefore have forced a heavily committed multi-front empire to keep precisely the remote bridgeheads KI#186.2 was intended to avoid.

`SASGameRecord` was decisive for this check because it separated who actually captured/razed each city, distinguished `AUTO_RAZE` from AI-selected razes, and exposed power, war, victory-stage, city-count, and Domination-progress context in the same chronology. The BBAI log for this particular run did not contain the detailed raze-decision diagnostics, so it was not needed to reach this conclusion. If the keep rule is broadened later, actual closeness to the Domination land/population thresholds remains a better candidate than generic military strength.

Fixed/investigated with the help of ChatGPT-5.6-Sol thanks.

## KI#187 - (Fixed/Improved) Base AdvCiv excessively devalued soon-connectable bonuses in AI city-site scoring

Base AdvCiv reduced a city site's non-yield bonus value to 70% when the bonus was not connectable yet but its required technology was currently researchable, and to roughly one third otherwise. AdvCiv-SAS initially preserved these inherited discounts when KI#178 replaced broad trade-style `AI_bonusVal` scoring with explicit long-term health/happiness settlement value.

The old split was not a good fit for permanent city-site evaluation. `canResearch()` only says that a technology can currently be selected; it does not measure whether the AI is researching it, how many turns remain, or how strategically distant the benefit is. Conversely, a visible early bonus could lose 30% despite requiring only another technology in the same era.

Save-file 453 made this especially clear. Spain evaluated the Incense near Barcelona at only 70% because it did not yet have Calendar, then completed Calendar on the same turn that it founded Barcelona. The log therefore called the bonus merely "soon" connectable and reduced its explicit health/happiness value from 325 to 228 immediately before the required same-era technology arrived. The resulting Barcelona site was still good and reached population 10, 15 production, and 35 commerce by turn 150, but the inherited penalty itself did not describe the actual long-term delay.

Replace the binary 70% / roughly-one-third rule with a simple XML-tunable era-distance adjustment:

- an earliest valid connection in the current or an earlier era keeps 100% health/happiness settlement value;
- each later era loses `SAS_EVALUATE_NON_YIELD_BONUS_CONNECTION_ERA_VALUE_LOSS_PERCENT`, currently 15%;
- therefore one era ahead receives 85%, two eras ahead 70%, and three eras ahead 55%;
- the result is clamped only at 0% to avoid negative value in unusual modmods.

The required connection era is the earliest era in which any valid non-Fort improvement can connect the bonus. For each valid improvement path, use the latest era among the bonus reveal technology, bonus city-trade technology, improvement build technology, and any technology needed to remove the plot's feature; then choose the earliest of those valid paths. This keeps the formula generic for XML changes and modmods instead of hardcoding Calendar resources or specific improvements.

Most bonuses that are already visible in the current AdvCiv-SAS XML can be connected in the current era or earlier, so they now retain their full long-term health/happiness value even when the exact technology has not been completed. Local improvement yields remain handled separately by the existing improvement-availability and bonus-yield scoring paths, and difficult access from another landmass remains a separate inherited adjustment.

Added detailed BBAI timing diagnostics with the current era, earliest connection era, era distance, XML loss per era, and resulting timing percentage for testing.

Fixed/improved with the help of GPT-5.6-Sol (on ChatGPT Codex) thanks.

## KI#188 - (Fixed/Improved) Major Base AdvCiv/K-Mod bug in organizing armies against Barbarian cities could park 65-82% of an AI's military or prevent capable attackers from forming city-assault expeditions

Screenshots/files for this issue: [google drive folder link](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1r__V2DklSbDwdxqCrmbvILlGSApYo6sA?usp=sharing).

SASGameRecord and BBAI logging exposed a major military-efficiency failure. Strong AIs could accumulate most of their army in one city-attack group while at peace, often inside a city, yet count very few units as an active field army. In the baseline save-file 453 run, the largest observed groups included 201 Scandinavian units (82% of its military), 95 Aztec units (65%), and 62 Sumerian units (77%). Sumer also had only 2 units counted as field army around turn 190 while a large concentration remained in Susa after conquest.

This was not harmless preparation. An army sitting together for many turns still costs maintenance, loses the opportunity to capture weak nearby Barbarian cities or pressure rivals, and lets opponents catch up to a temporary military advantage. It can also leave the rest of the empire inflexible: most units are nominally available, but concentrated in a group that has decided neither to attack nor to disperse.

The primary cause was an unfinished Base AdvCiv rule in `CvUnitAI::AI_attackCityMove` (`advc.300`). When an AI was at peace, not ready for a sneak attack, and effectively hunting only Barbarian cities, Base AdvCiv accepted a stack only below three times the estimated Barbarian garrison. Its own nearby comment already said that an oversized stack should perhaps be split. Instead, exceeding the maximum made the stack "not ready." The generic not-ready behavior could then wait for or attract still more units, making the exact condition that blocked movement progressively worse.

K-Mod grouping behavior amplified this Base AdvCiv problem. `AI_omniGroup` can merge multiple UnitAI roles into an attack-city group and can add a stack-of-doom allowance. Initially capping only the obvious `AI_attackCityMove` grouping calls reduced but did not remove repeated merge/split behavior. A dedicated diagnostic later recorded 166 grouping decisions that would bypass the expedition cap: 113 came from `UNITAI_COUNTER`, 48 from other `UNITAI_ATTACK_CITY` groups through late fallback grouping, and 5 from `UNITAI_CITY_DEFENSE`. This proved that caller-by-caller caps would remain fragile.

A separate K-Mod role-coordination issue could prevent an expedition from forming at all. SASGameRecord found early armies with 9-14 `UNITAI_ATTACK` units in an area but no `UNITAI_ATTACK_CITY` unit. Those broad attackers could capture cities, but K-Mod normally separates friendly-territory `UNITAI_ATTACK` groups of four or more down to two units and only occasionally directs them toward cities. Without one attack-city leader, substantial raw military strength could therefore remain fragmented instead of becoming a coordinated expedition.

The fix addresses both failures:

- The former three-times-garrison boundary is preserved as an XML-tunable expedition maximum, with the estimated attackers needed as the minimum useful cap.
- Oversized groups are partitioned into independently useful expeditions instead of being marked not ready. Actual attack and city-capture capability counts regardless of UnitAI label, and splitting proceeds only when the original group has enough total capability to provision the planned expeditions. `splitGroup` preserves proportional UnitAI and unit-type composition.
- The peaceful expedition cap is enforced centrally inside `AI_omniGroup` whenever any UnitAI tries to group with `UNITAI_ATTACK_CITY`. This covers current and future callers instead of depending on each caller to duplicate the cap. Active wars, sneak-attack readiness, turtle strategy, and contexts not focused on Barbarian hunting retain normal wartime grouping and stack-of-doom behavior.
- If an area has enough floating `UNITAI_ATTACK` units and a reachable Barbarian city but no `UNITAI_ATTACK_CITY` unit, one suitable attacker that can capture cities and has positive attack-city value becomes the missing leader. Ordinary city-defense claims still run first.

The iterative diagnostics also verified why central enforcement was necessary. Early versions produced 1,154 repeated split rows because groups immediately reunited; capping one same-plot path reduced this only to 1,010, broader attack-city caller caps to 388/385, and a diagnostic run still found the three bypassing UnitAI sources above. After centralizing the cap, the confirming `BBAI_20260717T061839Z_load1.log` contained only 23 split events across turns 102-271. They were isolated responses to genuine oversized groups or later changes in the dynamic cap, not the previous turn-after-turn 5+1 merge/split loop.

The same confirming `SASGameRecord_20260717T061839Z_load1.log` showed Scythian, Minoan, Khoisan, and Libyan captured on turns 70, 77, 90, and 123. No parking row used `readinessReason=barbarian_above_max`; 171 of 182 logged parking decisions considered the stack ready. Large concentration remained possible when appropriate: Scandinavia still had a 159-unit attack-city group at turn 270, then partitioned it once the peaceful Barbarian-only branch processed it. Sumer still had 78 field-army units at turn 270 and won the Space Race on turn 273, providing a useful sanity check that the fix did not broadly fragment normal military strength.

The main tuning points are `SAS_AI_BARBARIAN_CITY_EXPEDITION_MAX_GARRISON_MULTIPLIER` and `SAS_AI_BARBARIAN_CITY_EXPEDITION_CREATE_MISSING_LEADER_ENABLE`. The first controls peaceful expedition size; the second can disable the missing-leader conversion for compatibility testing.

Fixed/improved with the help of GPT-5.6-Sol (on ChatGPT Codex) thanks.

<a id="ki-188.2"></a>

## KI#188.2 - (Fixed/Improved) Base AdvCiv/K-Mod issue: offensive armies could ignore nearby endangered cities instead of going back to try to help defending them

This is a wartime-defense follow-up to KI#188. That investigation began with armies parking instead of using a temporary military advantage. Once SASGameRecord recorded army concentration and BBAI recorded attack-stack decisions, the same evidence raised the opposite deployment question: when an AI is invaded or backstabbed, can an offensive army interrupt its expedition or send part of the group home before an underdefended city falls?

The existing movement order did not handle this consistently. General attackers had some local defensive behavior, but a ready city-assault army could select another enemy city before K-Mod's later defensive-area checks. An army already in enemy territory could therefore continue its expedition even when one of its owner's endangered cities was reachable within a few turns. Sending the whole army home every time would also be wasteful: a sufficiently large expedition should be able to spare the defenders actually needed and continue applying pressure with the rest.

`BBAI_20260717T090854Z_load1.log` / `SASGameRecord_20260717T090854Z_load1.log` showed the clearest original failure. On turn 213, Baghdad needed 12 defenders and had 5, while a healthy 11-unit Arabian city-assault group was only two turns away in Kufah. The group waited for more units instead of helping Baghdad, grew to 23 units / 32% of Arabia's military, and attacked Prague. Baghdad fell on turn 213, Prague was not captured, and the army eventually turned back and retook Baghdad on turn 218 after its population had fallen from 10 to 4. Most other diagnostic rows were harmless shortages in safe cities or already-hopeless defenses, so the response needed to recognize real danger rather than recall armies for every routine garrison request.

The new response runs before a new offensive target is selected:

- In an area classified as defensive, the whole group first tries to counter a suitable reachable invader.
- Otherwise, or if no such counterattack is selected, it searches only endangered own cities reachable within three turns and subtracts defenders already assigned to arrive there.
- If the rescue is feasible, it detaches enough defend-capable units to fill the remaining shortage while leaving the rest of the offensive group intact. Mobile attackers without defensive bonuses can still help in this explicit emergency.
- A new rescue is rejected if a singleton cannot fill a shortage larger than one, or if the shortage would consume more than three quarters of a larger group. This avoids dissolving nearly the whole expedition for a defense that the group still cannot make adequate.
- Existing doomed-city evacuation still runs first, so this does not force units back into a city the AI has already decided to abandon.

The first implementation exposed two mission-coordination failures. In `BBAI_20260717T094555Z_load1.log`, Zulu groups responded to Kufah five times on turn 274 even though its remaining shortage was only one, because mobile units without defensive bonuses inherited ordinary `AI_guardCity` behavior and received no guard-city mission marker. Later groups therefore did not count them as incoming. The explicit emergency response now assigns `MISSIONAI_GUARD_CITY` even to those mobile attackers, while ordinary guard calls retain their old behavior. In `BBAI_20260717T105127Z_load1.log`, a later lifecycle issue remained: France's group 4448323 detached 11 units for Orleans on turn 274, then later on the same turn reused four of those exact units for Memphis. Some were redirected again toward other cities on later turns. Those units had received `MISSIONAI_GUARD_CITY`, but UnitAI-specific grouping could still run before the assignment continued and merge them back into an offensive group.

Fixing that required preserving the assignment, not merely issuing it:

- targeted guard-city missions now continue centrally before the individual land UnitAI movement routines, covering `UNITAI_ATTACK`, `UNITAI_ATTACK_CITY`, `UNITAI_COUNTER`, and other military roles;
- the explicit city target remains attached to emergency defenders after they arrive, protecting the assignment while the city remains endangered and short of defenders;
- ordinary stationary garrisons use their unchanged targetless guard missions and do not enter this emergency continuation path;
- when the danger or shortage ends, normal UnitAI movement can reuse the units.

The iterative logs were important because two superficially reasonable versions were still wrong. An over-broad central check in `BBAI_20260717T110936Z_load1.log` routed ordinary stationary garrisons through the emergency response, producing 1,188 actions and 1,013 `redirect_group_head` rows. Restricting continuation to explicitly targeted missions fixed that, but `BBAI_20260717T113100Z_load1.log` exposed one final collective-action problem at Chichen Itza: a group of 8 detached 6 defenders on turn 151, then each resulting singleton independently rejected the remaining shortage as too large, regrouped, and was detached again on turn 153; the city fell on turn 154. The initial three-quarter feasibility gate now applies only when creating a new rescue. Units already assigned to the same city continue their collective rescue even though no individual singleton could fill the whole remaining shortage alone.

The exact Baghdad history diverged in subsequent runs, so it could not be directly replayed after the cure. The confirming `BBAI_20260717T114542Z_load1.log` instead verified the corrected behavior in analogous endangered-city responses and contained 168 priority actions: 16 whole-group invader counters, 16 expedition splits, 10 group-head redirects, and 126 explicit guard-city continuations. Its 215 detached-unit rows represented 89 new assignments and 126 continuations. No short-interval fresh reassignment of the same unit to the same city remained. On turn 182, Amsterdam needed 12 defenders and had 5; a nearby 18-unit Dutch army detached the exact 7-unit shortage and retained 11 units. The reinforcements continued into Amsterdam on turn 183, and the first emergency ended. When a genuinely new emergency appeared on turn 193, Amsterdam needed 13 defenders and had 3; a 19-unit army sent 10 and retained 9. `SASGameRecord_20260717T114542Z_load1.log` showed that Amsterdam survived through the test. This confirms that emergency defenders can complete their mission without permanently freezing ordinary garrisons or needlessly dissolving every offensive army.

Fixed/improved with the help of GPT-5.6-Sol (on ChatGPT Codex) thanks.

## KI#188.3 - (Fixed/Improved) Major Base AdvCiv/K-Mod bug: city-assault armies without a reachable target or war plan could keep waiting for reinforcements indefinitely and park 40-53% of an AI's military

This is a peacetime follow-up to KI#188. The original cure stopped an oversized civilization AI expedition against a Barbarian city from being declared unready merely because it had more units than its weak target required. Later BBAI diagnostics showed a separate Base AdvCiv/K-Mod failure: a city-assault army could have no selected rival city, no pathable Barbarian city, and no war plan, yet continue using generic reinforcement-wait behavior instead of returning its excess units to other military duties.

This affects ordinary civilization AIs, not the Barbarian player. Barbarian cities matter here because an AI civilization at peace with every rival can still attack an independent Barbarian city without starting a normal war. If no such city is reachable either, the army has nothing useful to attack. The cure does not change how Barbarian units move or how civilization AIs respond to Barbarian units attacking their territory.

The clearest baseline example was the United States in save file 450. Its group grew from 6 units on turn 126 to 18 of the empire's 47 military units by turn 225 while still peaceful, without a target or war plan. The group then fought during a short war, showing that retaining a prepared nucleus was useful, but it returned to peace still holding 21 of 51 military units on turn 247. Repeatedly committing that much of the army before and after a war was not useful when no target existed. Those units still cost maintenance and could not flexibly defend other cities, form another expedition, or exploit a different opportunity.

The Netherlands showed the upper end of the title's measured range: 22 of its 41 military units (53%) were parked without a target or war plan on turn 219, then the group immediately became useful after the empire was attacked on turn 220. This again showed that the army itself was valuable once a real need appeared; the bug was committing most of it to reinforcement waiting before that need existed.

Three related behaviors sustained the parking:

- K-Mod's generic waits for incoming group members could return before the no-target path completed, even though the army had neither a selected city nor a war plan.
- After normal rival-city selection and the pathable-Barbarian fallback both failed, Base AdvCiv/K-Mod had no deliberate action for releasing a targetless peaceful army.
- General attackers and other military UnitAI roles released from the group could be attracted back through `AI_omniGroup`, rebuilding the same concentration.

The cure preserves preparation without keeping the whole army unavailable:

- Reinforcement waits now require either a selected target city or an actual war plan. A peaceful group with neither continues through the no-target handling instead of waiting merely because more units are approaching.
- After both normal and Barbarian target selection fail, an army at peace with no war plan releases excess units once it is safely inside its owner's territory and the plot is not threatened. It is not fragmented in foreign territory or immediate danger.
- The group head and a useful nucleus remain together. The retained size is the larger of `SAS_AI_TARGETLESS_PEACEFUL_ATTACK_CITY_GROUP_MIN_UNITS` and the estimated number of attackers needed against Barbarian cities.
- Units already assigned to other military roles are detached first. Only excess `UNITAI_ATTACK_CITY` units with positive general-attack value are converted to `UNITAI_ATTACK`, so units unsuitable for ordinary attack duties are not discarded from their specialist role.
- While there is no war plan, the central `AI_omniGroup` cap prevents released units from immediately rebuilding the parked group. Active wars, war plans, sneak-attack readiness, and turtle strategy retain normal large-army grouping.

The confirming save-file 450 run logged 59 releases across eight civilizations. All 357 detachments or reassignments reached the intended retained limit, with no unreleased excess; 327 units already had other military roles and only 30 genuine city-assault units required conversion. The United States groups were reduced from 13 to 11 units and later from 12 to 11. When a real war appeared, normal concentration still worked: Carthage combined a 63-unit army and advanced toward Susa.

Save file 452 independently confirmed the behavior with 93 releases across ten civilizations and 463 detachments or reassignments, again with no unreleased excess. Of those, 439 units already had other military roles and only 24 city-assault units were converted. Japan's targetless peaceful group was reduced from 21 to 11. Wartime armies remained unrestricted: China assembled roughly 180-202 units for its attack on Aksum, and several other empires launched 40-57-unit offensives. When peace followed Aksum's capture, the Chinese army immediately began splitting; China then adopted another war plan on the following turn, so it was free to regroup rather than being incorrectly dismantled during renewed preparation.

Fixed/improved with the help of GPT-5.6-Sol (on ChatGPT Codex) thanks.

## KI#188.3.2 - (Fixed/Improved) Base AdvCiv/K-Mod targetless army parking across several groups could concentrate 71 units (68% of an AI's military) in low-value Mainz while much stronger Aachen and Nuremberg held only 4 each

Some time after KI#188.3, new BBAI army-concentration diagnostics and SASGameRecord city snapshots showed that its first cure had not covered another form of the inherited Base AdvCiv/K-Mod failure. The inherited logic still caused targetless armies to wait for and attract reinforcements, but our first cure limited each city-assault group separately and did not limit several individually compliant groups parked together. This was an incomplete cure of the Base issue, not targetless army parking newly introduced by AdvCiv-SAS: the group sizes changed, but the inherited concentration could persist through a different group structure.

The new diagnostics exposed this remaining failure in a save-file 450 run. On turn 190, Holy Rome was at peace and concentrated 71 of its 105 military units (68%) in Mainz across 12 groups even though the largest group contained only the permitted 9 units. Mainz was Holy Rome's sixth city, founded on turn 117; it was only population 9, produced 14 production and 23 commerce, and had only 2 of its 6 worked plots improved. Meanwhile, stronger earlier cities were left thinly defended: the capital and first city, population-17 Aachen, produced 48 production and 53 commerce but held only 4 military units; the fourth city, population-15 Nuremberg, was founded on turn 62, produced 57 production, and also held only 4 military units. Prague and Vienna each held only 3. Thus the uncovered Base edge case committed most of the empire's army to a relatively low-value later city while leaving much more valuable cities with only small garrisons.

The retained limit now applies to the combined number of units belonging to all city-assault-led groups on the same safe owned plot. The release path can process several groups until only the useful nucleus remains, while `AI_omniGroup` prevents another merge from exceeding the combined limit in the first place. This does not cap ordinary defenders or general attackers merely located in the same city. It also retains the original safety boundaries: armies in foreign territory or immediate danger are not divided, and active wars, war plans, ready surprise attacks, and turtle strategy can still assemble large forces.

The preventive gate was important rather than merely an optimization. A first release-only test corrected Mainz, but produced 591 release events and detached 1,746 units already assigned to other military roles because some of the same groups repeatedly attracted and then released reinforcements, up to 65 times for one group. With the preventive gate, the next save-file 450 run fell to 78 releases and 331 such detachments, with at most four releases for one group. Mainz had only 7 units in 7 separate groups on turn 190 instead of 71 units, while real war plans still assembled armies up to 47 units. Save file 449 independently confirmed the result with only 44 releases and 108 detachments; its most-repeated group received six small corrections spread across 55 turns, each returning the combined total directly to 9, while a wartime army still reached 57 units. The remaining release events therefore serve as a safety net when a former war army becomes targetless or another grouping path creates excess, rather than sustaining a join-and-release loop.

Fixed/improved with the help of GPT-5.6-Sol (on ChatGPT Codex) thanks.

## KI#188.3.3 - (Fixed/Improved) Base AdvCiv/K-Mod issue: upgrade-city routing ignored affordability and helped concentrate up to 72% of an AI's military in one city while units waited up to 63 turns (aggravated by its mismatch with AdvCiv-SAS economic-return gates)

The Base AdvCiv source confirms the inherited mismatch directly. `CvUnit::getUpgradeCity` explicitly does not check whether the owner has enough gold because its comment says that `CvUnit::canUpgrade` handles affordability. However, `CvUnitAI::AI_travelToUpgradeCity` called only `getUpgradeCity`, moved toward the selected city without calling `canUpgrade`, and issued `MISSION_SKIP` every turn once the unit arrived. AdvCiv-SAS later added economic-return gates to `canUpgrade`, which can reject an affordable upgrade when its military improvement is not worth its price, but the inherited travel-and-wait decision ignored those results too. Thus the underlying Base/K-Mod issue remained and the later AdvCiv-SAS checks made the mismatch substantially worse: a unit could travel to a crowded city and keep skipping turns for an upgrade that the AI could not afford or had already decided not to buy.

BBAI diagnostics in save file 450 recorded 1,081 crowded-city candidate checks and 1,053 waits. Of the candidate checks, 372 lacked enough gold and 631 had enough gold but failed the actual AdvCiv-SAS economic gates; only 78 were currently eligible to upgrade. For up to 63 turns, the logs repeatedly recorded the same units being sent toward crowded upgrade cities or forced to skip their turns once there. Those units therefore could not attack, reinforce another city, reposition for defense, or perform any other military duty on those turns; only 53 of 99 such units were eventually upgraded. The affected cities included New York with 42 of the United States' 58 military units and Mainz with 99 of Holy Rome's 144. Other army-organization problems also contributed to those concentrations, but upgrade routing repeatedly held or returned units there instead of letting their normal roles use them.

The upgrade-city search now optionally returns the exact upgrade type it selected. When the unit can currently move in owned territory, `AI_travelToUpgradeCity` applies the real affordability and economic-return checks to that exact upgrade before travelling or waiting. A rejected unit resumes its normal military role until the upgrade becomes genuinely available. Foreign-territory travel remains allowed because failing `canUpgrade` there reflects the unit's current position rather than an economic rejection. The added known-city parameter prevents the eligibility check from incorrectly testing only the nearest city after the broader search has already found another suitable upgrade city.

In the corrected save-file 450 run, crowded-city waits fell from 1,053 to 9, involving only 5 units, and all 5 were upgraded shortly afterward; the cure also released 198 rejected candidates and prevented 91 unnecessary journeys. Save file 449 independently recorded 328 releases and 214 prevented journeys. Its only 22 waits involved 14 units: every unit that waited before the final turn was upgraded soon afterward, while the remaining 6 waited after Zulu had already spent 354 of its 376-gold upgrade budget on turn 319 and had no next turn because Carthage won on turn 320. The cure therefore removes indefinite rejected-upgrade parking without disrupting useful short waits for upgrades the AI is actively purchasing.

Fixed/improved with the help of GPT-5.6-Sol (on ChatGPT Codex) thanks.

## KI#188.4 - (Fixed) Base AdvCiv/K-Mod bug: AI armies preparing war against a civilization could still be classified as hunting only Barbarian cities

This is a war-preparation follow-up to KI#188. Base AdvCiv/K-Mod decided that a civilization AI was hunting only Barbarian cities when it was at peace and its sneak attack was not yet ready. The condition did not check whether a real war plan already existed. The preparation period before `AI_isSneakAttackReady` therefore still used Barbarian-expedition readiness even though the empire had already selected a rival and was mobilizing for that war.

The distinction matters because an army sufficient for a weak Barbarian garrison is not necessarily sufficient for a civilization war. KI#188 also deliberately limits peaceful Barbarian expeditions so they do not absorb most of an empire's military; applying that smaller-expedition context during a real war preparation could make armies move, split, or wait according to the wrong objective instead of reaching normal war-stack readiness.

Save-file 450 BBAI logging exposed the exact overlap. Hannibal was preparing a total war against nearby Willem, whose power was about 54% of Carthage's, but several Carthaginian city-assault groups still entered the Barbarian-only branch. After adding the missing no-war-plan requirement, turn-166, turn-172, and turn-174 groups with 6, 7, and 9 units respectively logged `huntOnlyBarbs=0` and `readinessReason=war_below_needed`, using the normal 10- or 17-unit war requirement rather than the smaller Barbarian estimate.

The fix adds `!bAnyWarPlan` to the inherited Barbarian-only classification. Peaceful Barbarian expeditions remain unchanged when no rival war is planned, while every active preparation now uses real-war readiness before `AI_isSneakAttackReady` becomes true. A separate ready 11-unit Carthaginian army still selected distant Scythian afterward, proving that target quality and readiness classification were distinct problems; that strategic follow-up is KI#188.5.

Fixed with the help of GPT-5.6-Sol (on ChatGPT Codex) thanks.

<a id="ki-188.5"></a>

## KI#188.5 - (Improved) AI armies could waste their strength razing distant Barbarian cities instead of leaving Barbarian pressure to weaken nearer rivals and remaining available for offense or defense

KI#188.4 fixed the inherited readiness classification, but a fully ready army could still select any pathable Barbarian city. BBAI and SASGameRecord testing showed that this was strategically harmful when the city was far from the attacker and unlikely to be retained. The attacker paid unit-production opportunity, mobilization, travel, combat, healing, maintenance, and lost-tempo costs, yet razing the city removed military pressure from the nearer rival and cleared a future settlement site for that rival. Leaving the Barbarian city alive can instead force the rival to fight it, defend against it, delay expansion, or spend its own Settler and development time.

The clearest baseline was population-3 Libyan in save file 450. On turn 74, AdvCiv-SAS created a Carthaginian Barbarian-expedition leader for a seven-turn route. Hannibal spent 16 turns reaching and capturing Libyan, razed it at population 5 on turn 90, and Shaka founded Bulawayo on the exact `(10,41)` plot only 10 turns later. Hannibal therefore paid the entire military and tempo cost while preparing Shaka's next city site. A separate ready 11-unit Carthaginian army selected population-9 Scythian about 10 path turns and 22 plots away while Carthage was preparing against Willem; Arabia captured and razed Scythian on turn 179 before Hannibal could benefit.

AdvCiv-SAS now rejects only a Barbarian target that is both farther than the XML-tunable `SAS_AI_BARBARIAN_CITY_EXPEDITION_MAX_DISPOSABLE_PATH_TURNS_UNSCALED_GAMESPEED` and unlikely to benefit its attacker long-term. The default permits targets within 3 path turns because quick conquest gold, experience, immediate security, or denying a nearby site can repay a short expedition. Beyond that grace distance, the shared KI#186 `AI_isSASCityLikelyToBenefitUsLongTerm` evaluation must say the city is worth keeping. This preserves intrinsically valuable or sustainably located Barbarian cities instead of using a blanket distance ban.

The gate covers all three routes that produced expeditions: ordinary city targeting, KI#188's missing Barbarian-expedition-leader creation, and the no-target Barbarian fallback. When ordinary targeting rejects a city, it retries without Barbarian candidates so an available civilization target can replace it. If none exists, the existing defensive, staging, targetless-release, and future-opportunity logic remains available instead of committing the army to the rejected expedition.

The confirming `BBAI_20260720T074947Z_load1.log` and matching SASGameRecord reproduced the intended dynamic behavior. Hannibal rejected Libyan from turn 74 while it was distant and unlikely to benefit Carthage long-term. His strength remained available, and Carthage captured Medina, Baghdad, uMgungundlovu, Nobamba, and Damascus from turns 168-195. Shaka meanwhile fought multiple Barbarian units around Libyan without capturing the city. Once Carthage's new conquests brought the site within its sustainable empire, the long-term result changed from reject to keep; Hannibal captured and retained population-7 Libyan on turn 204, then captured and retained population-7 Scythian on turn 208. Thus the cure delayed the conquest while it primarily helped a rival, then allowed it once the same cities had become durable Carthaginian gains.

The first diagnostic prototype produced 4,679 repetitive evaluation rows because the existing opportunity logger inspected the same candidates for many armies every turn. Diagnostic-only inspection now bypasses the behavioral filter, while the decision log records only the first result and later keep/reject transitions for each player and Barbarian city. The identical confirming run produced 19 rows without changing the gameplay outcome.

Improved with the help of GPT-5.6-Sol (on ChatGPT Codex) thanks.
