## KI#198.2 - (Fixed/Improved) Base AdvCiv AI non-combat food-production allocation could stall small growing cities instead of using mature or stagnant food/production pumps (observed with Workers)

Follow-up to KI#198. The underlying allocation behavior is inherited from Base AdvCiv: after a city decided that a food-production civilian was wanted, there was no central cross-city check asking whether that city was a sensible place to freeze growth while training it. AdvCiv-SAS's stronger Worker floor made this long-standing inefficiency much easier to observe because Workers were requested more reliably.

A young population-1/2 city could therefore spend 10-40+ turns on a Worker even when a mature city on the same landmass could convert much more food plus production into the same unit in only a few turns. This did not reduce the requested Worker count; it made the empire pay for that Worker with unnecessarily expensive lost growth and delayed use. Workers provide the empirical reproduction, but the optimization belongs at the generic non-combat food-production layer rather than in Worker-specific production branches.

There had been related older work, which explains why this issue could feel familiar without actually having been solved generically. AdvCiv-SAS had already restricted Settler production to the capital/high population specifically to exploit food-is-production efficiently and avoid small cities spending many turns stalled on Settlers. That older Settler rule addresses the same economic principle through a specialized restriction.

Conversely, the later KI#198 Worker-floor change deliberately did not restrict Workers to only high-population/capital cities because weaker or stagnant cities can sometimes contribute efficiently and because broad restrictions could slow emergency replacement. What was still missing was a central cross-city comparison after a fresh non-combat food-production choice had already passed its ordinary need/priority/odds logic.

The new allocation rule is therefore a gate rather than a fixed-city restriction. For a fresh non-combat food-production unit, any safe city that can finish within `SAS_AI_CHOOSE_UNIT_NONCOMBAT_FOOD_PRODUCTION_MAX_TURNS_NORMAL_GAMESPEED` (6 Normal-speed-equivalent turns by default after the Worker-cost restoration, originally 5 while the standard Worker cost was 50, scaled by game-speed `TrainPercent`) is already considered good enough and keeps the choice immediately.

This intentionally allows multiple cities to rebuild Workers in parallel after heavy losses. Existing invested production is also always completed. Only a slower fresh choice looks for another safe city on the same landmass that can train the unit at least as quickly; if no such city exists, the current/best available producer still builds instead of waiting.

Among eligible alternatives, population and stagnation choose the preferred food/hammer pump rather than a fragile turns-saved formula. The largest eligible population is the default preference, because larger cities can usually convert much more food and hammer output while the unit freezes growth.

However, a currently stagnant city is preferred when it is within `SAS_AI_CHOOSE_UNIT_NONCOMBAT_FOOD_PRODUCTION_STAGNANT_POPULATION_GAP` of that largest city (3 by default, using a strict comparison: population 8 can beat population 10, population 7 cannot). This makes otherwise-unused food productive and deliberately allows a strong stagnant pump to build several Workers in sequence. Actual production turns only provide the fast-enough/sanity gate and equal-population tie-break; they are not the strategic score.

The implementation is generic for non-combat `isFoodProduction()` units and excludes combat-capable, air-combat and nuclear units so a future modmod that creates a food-production fighter is not unnecessarily constrained. Workers are the important currently affected unit in AdvCiv-SAS. Settlers are conceptually part of the same food-production allocation problem, but `UNITAI_SETTLE` is currently exempt because AdvCiv-SAS separately allows Settlers only from the capital.

Without the exemption, the capital could defer a Settler to a non-capital that current production policy would never actually request to build it. The existing capital-only Settler rule therefore remains the specialized Settler solution for now. If that restriction is later removed, this generic allocator can take over Settler allocation by removing that one role exemption.

The full `BBAI_20260809T054807Z_load1.log` / `SASGameRecord_20260809T054807Z_load1.log` validation ran through turn 391. The new allocator produced 87 actual `DEFER_TO_PREFERRED_CITY` decisions. Their median source city was population 2 with a 9-turn Worker, while the median preferred city was population 8 with a 3-turn Worker.

Representative cases included Memphis population 1 / 12 turns -> Thebes population 5 / 4 turns, New York population 1 / 15 -> Washington population 5 / 3, Nippur population 1 / 15 -> Babylon population 8 / 4, and Huamanga population 1 / 45 -> Cuzco population 11 / 3. Of the 87 redirects, 48 selected a stagnant preferred city, showing that the stagnation preference materially affects allocation rather than merely documenting intent.

The opposite safety behavior was also directly visible. There were 63 KEEP decisions from population-4-or-smaller cities that could complete the Worker within the 5-turn Normal-speed gate, confirming that efficient side cities still participate in rapid replacement. The allocator also did not create a waiting deadlock: of 85 deferrals with enough later log history to observe another allocation event before game end, all 85 saw that empire reach a later KEEP Worker decision within 5 turns and 80 did so within 2 turns.

Worker availability remained high in the GameRecord as well; for example, the USA had 11 Workers for 6 cities at turn 100 with 9 actively building improvements, while India later had 24 Workers at turn 300. The change therefore improves which city pays the food-production growth cost rather than lowering the KI#198 Worker force.

`FOOD_PRODUCTION_ALLOCATION` remains available through the dedicated Worker BBAI log: level 2 records the unusual deferrals, while level 3 can additionally record ordinary KEEP decisions. The turn-391 diagnostic run temporarily used Worker log level 3 and produced a very large BBAI file mostly because the existing full Worker scan diagnostics are intentionally exhaustive; the committed/default Worker log level is restored to 0.

Update: The default was raised from 5 to 6 when the normal Worker cost was restored from 50 to 60, preserving the same approximate 10 production-equivalent-per-turn "fast enough" threshold (50 / 5 = 60 / 6 = 10) instead of accidentally making secondary Worker pumps 20% harder to qualify.

Fixed/improved with the help of GPT-5.6 Thinking thanks.

## KI#199 - (Fixed/Improved) Base AdvCiv/K-Mod generic UnitAI fallback could use dedicated land anti-air units as ordinary attackers or reserves

Primary empirical reproduction and validation: save file 459.

Save file 459 exposed a long-standing late-game composition problem in which dedicated land anti-air units could occupy a very large share of an AI army. In one run, Saladin had 108 combat units on turn 350, including 41 Mobile SAMs. BBAI production traces showed that this was not only legitimate anti-air demand: Mobile SAM was repeatedly selected for generic `UNITAI_ATTACK`, `UNITAI_ATTACK_CITY`, and `UNITAI_RESERVE` roles, and SAM Infantry could also leak into generic attack/reserve selection.

The XML already described the intended role clearly. Both SAM Infantry and Mobile SAM explicitly listed `UNITAI_COUNTER`, `UNITAI_CITY_COUNTER`, and `UNITAI_CITY_SPECIAL`, but their `NotUnitAIs` did not forbid the generic offensive/reserve roles. In `CvPlayerAI::AI_unitValue`, explicit `UnitAIs` are not an exclusive whitelist: if a combat-capable unit is not marked as mostly defensive, generic fallback logic can still consider it valid for `UNITAI_ATTACK`, `UNITAI_ATTACK_CITY`, `UNITAI_RESERVE` (and related generic roles) unless `NotUnitAIs` explicitly rejects that role. Mobile SAM's useful combat strength and 2 movement made that fallback particularly capable of competing with ordinary frontline units despite its intended anti-air specialization.

The fix is intentionally data-driven and small: SAM Infantry and Mobile SAM now explicitly add `UNITAI_ATTACK`, `UNITAI_ATTACK_CITY`, and `UNITAI_RESERVE` to `NotUnitAIs`. Their intended `UNITAI_COUNTER`, `UNITAI_CITY_COUNTER`, and `UNITAI_CITY_SPECIAL` entries remain unchanged, so the AI can still build and use them as anti-air/counter units. Save-file 459 follow-up BBAI logs showed no selections of either dedicated AA unit into the newly forbidden generic roles.

No blanket percentage cap on land anti-air units is added by this fix. A high anti-air share can still be legitimate if the AI's actual counter logic calls for it, and save file 459 also showed that substantial Mobile-SAM production can occur through `UNITAI_COUNTER`. If legitimate counter-role demand later proves systematically excessive, that can be tuned separately with evidence. This issue specifically fixes specialized AA units consuming ordinary offensive/reserve slots because of generic UnitAI fallback.

Fixed/improved with the help of GPT-5.6 Thinking thanks.

## KI#200 - (Improved) Inherited Base AdvCiv/K-Mod sacrifice selection could spend current units before SAS-defined obsolete expendables during risky AI stack attacks

The `WAR_ATTACK_ORDER` diagnostics retained from KI#197.9 exposed a separate attack-order interaction rather than another military-production issue. The provenance matters: the explicit unit `ObsoleteTech` field and the resulting concept of a unit being **obsolete** for this ordering are AdvCiv-SAS-specific; Base AdvCiv/K-Mod does not have that unit-obsolescence system. The later `AI_getBestGroupSacrifice()` fallback is inherited Base AdvCiv/K-Mod logic, so it naturally evaluates sacrifice value without knowing that SAS may already consider one candidate strategically obsolete. The two systems could therefore work against each other.

In one early direct example, the SAS low-power selector chose a 136-turn-old obsolete Archer at 10% odds, but inherited sacrifice selection replaced it with a 5-turn-old current Horse Archer. Across that diagnostic run, 189 logged attacks replaced an obsolete SAS-selected attacker with a non-obsolete final attacker, all through the sacrifice fallback. The important distinction is not the logged XP difference by itself: the obsolete Archer is a much weaker/outdated unit, while the current Horse Archer remains materially more useful. XP still has value, but it is intentionally not a standalone reason to preserve an obsolete unit; obsolete units are often poor-value upgrade candidates and may be more efficiently spent in war. The inherited sacrifice value remains important because it captures tactical utility and can prevent absurd substitutions, including logged cases where an obsolete unit had only 2% odds while a current Mechanized Infantry had 71%.

The cure therefore stays local to the AI sacrifice fallback rather than changing `AI_sacrificeValue()` globally or forcing all obsolete units to attack first. When inherited sacrifice selection chooses a non-obsolete unit below the configured safe-attack threshold, the AI searches the same group for an eligible obsolete alternative. The obsolete candidate must retain at least `SAS_AI_GETBESTGROUPATTACKER_OBSOLETE_SACRIFICE_MIN_VALUE_PERCENT_OF_CURRENT` of the inherited sacrifice value (70% as of now), and if the inherited sacrifice provides bombard or collateral capability the replacement must also provide one of those tactical roles. Obsolete means specifically that the unit's SAS XML `ObsoleteTech` has been reached; raw age does not qualify it, and raw XP does not override that status.

Attack odds are treated differently depending on how risky the inherited current-unit attack already is. Current-unit attacks at or above `SAS_AI_GETBESTGROUPATTACKER_OBSOLETE_SACRIFICE_CURRENT_SAFE_ODDS_PERCENT` (90% as of now) are left unchanged because the unit is very likely to survive. Above the risky-expenditure threshold, an obsolete replacement may be at most `SAS_AI_GETBESTGROUPATTACKER_OBSOLETE_SACRIFICE_MAX_ODDS_DEFICIT_PERCENT` percentage points worse (25 as of now). At or below `SAS_AI_GETBESTGROUPATTACKER_OBSOLETE_SACRIFICE_ODDS_DEFICIT_BYPASS_MAX_CURRENT_ODDS_PERCENT` (60% as of now), that odds-deficit cap is bypassed: the current unit is already being asked to take a materially risky fight, so a tactically credible obsolete unit can instead be used as an expendable or "cannon-fodder" attacker first. This can soften the defender, preserve the current unit for a safer follow-up, naturally remove obsolete excess and its unit-support burden, and avoid pressure to spend upgrade gold on units that may no longer justify it. All thresholds and the optimization itself are XML-tunable.

Several staged full-autoplay tests were used rather than adopting a blanket obsolete-first rule. Tight initial 80%-value and 15-point-odds gates proved the mechanism was very selective; later 70% and 25-point tests exposed more useful substitutions without making the rule dominate normal combat. One especially clear full-autoplay sequence on turn 330 preserved a Mechanized Infantry that initially had only 36% odds, spent an obsolete Horse Knight at 2% and then an obsolete Paratrooper at 7%, and after the Paratrooper damaged the Mobile SAM defender to 52 HP the same Mechanized Infantry was reevaluated at 99% and won without taking damage. This is the intended pattern: spend expendables while the current-unit attack is dangerous, then let the current unit take the safer finishing fight.

Save file 454 independently provided a broader sample. The run logged 29 obsolete-expenditure overrides among 1,426 non-Barbarian attack selections, and six choices genuinely required bypassing the normal 25-point deficit. Those six used current-unit odds of 38%, 50%, 48%, 37%, 43% and 38%; five obsolete replacements died and one withdrew, while the surviving defenders took 42, 57, 19, 0, 64 and 0 damage respectively. In two of those assaults the preserved current unit later attacked during the same turn and won without taking damage. A turn-152 obsolete Archer was particularly useful: it attacked instead of a 43% current Longbowman, withdrew after inflicting 64 damage, and the preserved Longbowman later won its own combat at 0 damage. Some cannon-fodder attacks still die without damaging the defender, which is expected rather than hidden: the feature deliberately chooses which unit pays for an already-risky attack; it does not guarantee that every expendable produces value.

The bypass threshold was subsequently raised from the directly exercised 50% boundary to 60% as a deliberately somewhat more aggressive cleanup policy. Two full runs made with the 60% setting produced no qualifying bypass case whose inherited current-unit odds were actually 51-60%, so that exact extra interval has not yet been isolated empirically. The mechanism itself is well exercised at lower risky odds, and the value remains XML-tunable for later balance adjustment without recompiling.

The detailed level-3 `WAR_ATTACK_ORDER` candidate and exact battle-ID diagnostics are retained for now so future tuning can distinguish ordinary sacrifice selection from obsolete-expenditure overrides and directly join selected units to combat outcomes.

Improved with the help of GPT-5.6 Thinking thanks.

## KI#201 - (Fixed/Improved) Base AdvCiv relative-strength tech-trade rubber-banding guaranteed weaker recipients discounts without bargaining risk

[The same CivFanatics player report](https://forums.civfanatics.com/threads/advciv-sas-simple-advanced-strategy.699716/post-16979072) that prompted the preceding [map-generation compatibility commit `d2c3107`](https://github.com/wonderingabout/AdvCiv-SAS/commit/d2c310774e5e93787c6609b01c9fb60880d6311c), and [another one of the same user](https://forums.civfanatics.com/threads/advciv-sas-simple-advanced-strategy.699716/post-16979573) also identified AdvCiv change 550a's relative-strength adjustment to technology trade values. Base BTS makes technology trade value independent of how well the recipient is doing. AdvCiv instead makes a weaker recipient value technology from a stronger civilization less, using a weighted average in which relative technology score counts twice as much as relative military power.

The adjustment grows with game progress. Its strongest possible discount is about 20% one quarter of the way through the estimated game, 33% halfway through and 50% at the estimated end turn. These are caps requiring a sufficiently large relative-strength difference, not the result of every trade. However, a late-game technology-for-technology exchange can consequently require the stronger side to offer up to roughly twice the ordinary nominal value. Large empire size is not measured directly, but a technologically leading large empire will often also have greater total military power and therefore receive the strongest form of the adjustment.

The central design problem is that this is not ordinary bargaining. `CvPlayerAI::AI_considerOffer` evaluates what each side receives through that recipient's `AI_dealVal`, which in turn calls the recipient team's `AI_techTradeVal`. Both AI sides therefore adopt the weaker recipient's discounted valuation as the fair price. The weaker AI does not risk making a stingy offer that the stronger AI may reject, nor decide whether the technology is urgent enough to justify paying the ordinary price or whether another seller is likely to appear. Against a human, the player can reject the artificial price, leaving the weaker AI without the technology; an ordinary rejected trade offer also does not itself create the diplomatic consequence that refusing a demand or plea can create. The rule is therefore a guaranteed AI-to-AI catch-up transfer rather than a model of strategically choosing when to bargain hard.

This is rubber-banding rather than merely a strategy change because the transaction's price is changed directly from the civilizations' relative technology score and military power: falling behind automatically makes incoming technology cheaper, being ahead removes that advantage, and the maximum intervention grows as the game progresses. It applies without first establishing that the technology is urgent, that competing sellers exist or that accepting less is in the stronger seller's interest. A strategy change would instead make the weaker AI search more actively, compare sellers, preserve resources when waiting is safe or pay the ordinary price when immediate acquisition has the better expected outcome, while leaving the other side independently free to accept or reject the proposed deal.

AdvCiv-SAS now controls this factor through `SAS_AI_TECH_TRADE_RELATIVE_STRENGTH_EFFECT_PERCENT`. The default `0` restores BTS strength-independent valuation for this factor; `100` restores the full AdvCiv adjustment, and intermediate values such as `30` or `50` proportionally soften it. When set to `0`, the power-ratio, technology-ratio and game-progress calculations are skipped. The setting does not disable independent AdvCiv-SAS technology-trade logic, including common-technology discounts, master-vassal-locus valuation or extra valuation of urgent military technologies. AdvCiv's existing exclusion for direct master-vassal relationships also remains unchanged when the effect is enabled.

The DLL compiled and an in-game smoke test ran successfully with the new default. Broader BBAI technology-trade diagnostics are deliberately postponed until after release: useful logging should connect contact selection, denials, candidate packages, individual valuation modifiers, counterproposals and the final accepted or rejected deal, rather than flooding the log with every speculative `AI_techTradeVal` call.

Fixed/improved based on the linked player report and with the help of GPT-5.6-Sol thanks.

## KI#202 - (Fixed) Base AdvCiv's uncapped second OneArea-resource pass could not revisit landmasses capped during its first pass

The map-generation audit preceding the previous [map-generation compatibility commit `d2c3107`](https://github.com/wonderingabout/AdvCiv-SAS/commit/d2c310774e5e93787c6609b01c9fb60880d6311c) also exposed a Base AdvCiv small bug: change `advc.129` relaxed BTS's single-landmass resource placement and added a first-pass limit of `2 + (area tiles / 25)` copies of a OneArea resource per area. Excess copies were intended to spread to other suitable areas first. A documented second pass then ignored this per-area limit so that the new distribution rule would not reduce the total number of resources when the first pass could not reach `calculateNumBonusesToAdd`'s target.

The second pass could not perform that intended fallback. Its `areas_tried` set was inherited from the earlier single-pass BTS/K-Mod algorithm, declared outside the new two-pass loop, and never cleared. Every area selected during the capped first pass therefore remained excluded during the uncapped second pass. The second pass could occasionally select an area that the first pass had never selected, including through a newly randomized positive area score, but it could not return to any area where the new cap had actually stopped placement. This could leave fewer OneArea resources than the calculated target even when those previously selected areas still contained valid plots.

AdvCiv-SAS now clears `areas_tried` when the uncapped second pass begins. The first pass still prefers spreading the resource across suitable areas and applies the inherited AdvCiv cap. Only when the target remains unmet does the second pass reconsider each area once without that cap; all ordinary tile eligibility, latitude, resource-spacing, clustering and target-count rules still apply, so genuinely impossible placements remain absent. The BTS alternative selected by disabling `SAS_MAP_ADVCIV_ONE_AREA_BONUS_DISTRIBUTION_ENABLE` still uses only its original single pass and is unchanged.

This affects XML bonuses with `bArea=1`, currently Banana, Maize, Cattle, Deer, Pig, Rice, Sheep, Wheat, Dye, Incense, Elephants, Silk, Spices, Sugar and Grapes in AdvCiv-SAS. It does not change their XML frequency settings or calculated targets; it changes whether the generator can fulfill those targets. When the capped first pass already reaches a bonus's target, the second pass does nothing and the direct result is unchanged. When the first pass undershoots and a previously selected area still has valid plots, the fixed second pass can place more copies of that bonus than the broken behavior did, but never more than the existing target. Those restored copies are placed on suitable areas that the first pass had already capped rather than remaining absent. Their exact locations, and potentially later resource placement through occupied plots and the advancing map random-number sequence, can consequently differ even though the target calculation itself is unchanged.

The defect was introduced in Base AdvCiv commit `f25a2b91a` when the area cap and two-pass fallback were added together; this fix is therefore a correction of that algorithm's documented intent rather than a new resource-distribution policy.

Update after the later C++ File Audit Album review: KI#202 remains a correct and necessary repair, but restoring the intended revisit path exposed a separate inherited scoring assumption. AdvCiv's denominator always counted the area's existing unique `OneArea` resource types "plus this one," which was correct only while an area already containing the current resource could never be revisited. On a KI#202 second-pass revisit, the live area counter already includes that resource, so the unconditional extra one counted it twice and could reduce a viable recovery area's score to zero. [KI#569](/_1_AdvCiv-SAS/Docs/README_Known_Issues.md#ki-569) updates the denominator for the restored lifecycle; KI#202 must not be reverted.

Fixed with the help of GPT-5.6-Sol thanks.

## KI#203 - (Improved) AI Auto Play could pause behind harmless informational popups, and its logs could not reliably explain why a run ended

Screenshots/files for this issue: [google drive folder link](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1wn3TmI3Hp8tUUQUubbVvPoo6cKRNO5Q1?usp=sharing).

AI Auto Play is used heavily for AdvCiv-SAS balance and AI testing, but two control-layer gaps made unattended runs less reliable and their results more tedious to verify. First, no-decision informational dialogs could wait indefinitely for the user to press OK. These include ordinary `BUTTONPOPUP_TEXT` notices and the EXE's active-player handoff/password prompt. Second, all completion paths ultimately reset the same autoplay counter to zero, so an `AUTOPLAY_ENDED` record could not reliably distinguish scheduled completion from manual interruption, victory, active-player defeat, desynchronization, an assertion, Rise & Fall control flow or another reset. Reviewers therefore had to infer whether the requested benchmark actually finished, and full autoplay automation would still require a user to clear harmless notices.

The first runtime test exposed the second popup path directly. At turn 304, the active player changed from player 0 to player 1 while autoplay still had 197 turns remaining, and the EXE displayed "Huayna Capac, it's your turn!" through `gDLL->getPassword`; this bypassed the generic `BUTTONPOPUP_TEXT` launcher gate. AdvCiv-SAS therefore now optionally omits both no-decision paths while AI Auto Play is active. `SAS_AIAUTOPLAY_AUTO_DISMISS_INFORMATIONAL_POPUPS_ENABLE` enables this by default. It deliberately does not auto-accept or suppress diplomacy, random events, civics, war, spaceship launch, city production, technology selection or any other popup that represents a gameplay or session decision.

The shared `SASAutoPlayEndCause` enum and a cause-aware Python-to-DLL stop method now preserve why automation ended. SASGameRecord records a request ID, requested and completed turns, start/current turn context, explicit end cause, and active-player changes during both the current request and the log session. Ordinary countdown ticks remain omitted to avoid one row per turn. This makes the autoplay boundary directly machine-readable and is also a step toward safely running future unattended AI benchmarks without requiring a human to interpret counter resets or press no-effect OK buttons.

The player-handoff follow-up compiled and the confirming full run completed without showing the prompt. Player 0 changed to player 1 on turn 392 while autoplay still had 109 turns remaining; `ACTIVE_PLAYER_CHANGED` recorded the exact transfer, and `AUTOPLAY_INFORMATIONAL_POPUP_DISMISSED` recorded `popupKind=PLAYER_HANDOFF_PASSWORD`. The final row reported `activePlayerChanges=1`, `totalActivePlayerChanges=1`, and `endCause=VICTORY`. Although 501 turns had been requested, it correctly reported 500 completed turns because a Time victory ended the run first.

A separate short test then exercised three requests in one log session. Request 1 scheduled 21 turns and reported all 21 completed with `endCause=SCHEDULED`. Request 2 scheduled 31 turns, was manually stopped with 13 remaining, and correctly reported 18 completed with `endCause=USER_INTERRUPTED`. Request 3 scheduled 61 turns and reported all 61 completed with `endCause=SCHEDULED`. Their request IDs advanced from 1 to 3 and each row preserved its own starting turn/elapsed-turn context. For scheduled runs, `elapsedGameTurns` is one lower than `completedTurns` because a request starting on turn 0 processes turns 0 through 20 inclusively while the game-turn counter advances by 20; `completedTurns` retains the requested 21-turn workload. An ordinary `BUTTONPOPUP_TEXT` suppression has not yet occurred naturally in a confirming log, but its no-action handler and shared launcher gate make it the simpler of the two suppression paths.

Improved with the help of GPT-5.6-Sol thanks.

<a id="ki-204"></a>

## KI#204 - (Fixed/Improved) Base AdvCiv Great General birth, safety and reporting gaps could waste free Great Generals, including unsafe birth-city selection and an inverted Military Academy city-safety test

A Great General investigation initially looked like it might mainly concern AdvCiv-SAS's balance choice to strongly prefer Military Instructors and largely suppress low-value combat-unit attachments. Comparing the current code with the latest available Base AdvCiv source and reviewing 15 recent SASGameRecord autoplay logs instead exposed a mixture of inherited AdvCiv problems, inherited limitations that benefit from hardening, SAS-specific balance policy and SAS logging/reporting gaps. The 15 reviewed logs contained 1,137 Great General births, 1,101 Military Instructor joins, 18 Military Academy constructions and 7 explicit deaths of the free `UNIT_GREAT_GENERAL` itself; 6 of the 7 deaths occurred in or immediately around cities that were already collapsing, while the seventh General moved out of Poverty Point and was killed by a Gunship on a non-city plot the next turn.

- **Fixed Base AdvCiv issue - unsafe automatic Great General birth city:** `CvPlayer::setCombatExperience` selected the automatic Great-General birth city from all cities using randomized yield/population ranks without checking city safety, so a defenseless General could be created directly in a besieged city despite safer cities existing. AdvCiv-SAS keeps the original scoring but restricts selection to safe cities whenever at least one safe city exists; if every city is unsafe, it falls back to the original all-city selection. The synchronized random roll is still consumed for every city before filtering so the safety correction does not unnecessarily alter the synchronized RNG stream.
- **Fixed Base AdvCiv bug - inverted Military Academy city-safety test:** `CvUnitAI::AI_construct` used `pLoopCity->AI_isSafe()` as a reason to reject a city, which skipped safe cities while leaving unsafe cities eligible for Military Academy targeting. This is now corrected to reject cities that are not safe, matching the nearby `AI_join` logic.
- **Hardened inherited AdvCiv/K-Mod limitation - movement flags were not tactical safety:** Great General joining relied on `MOVE_SAFE_TERRITORY`, whose pathfinder meaning is ownership/revelation safety rather than protection from attack on the actual end-turn plot; Academy movement had a similar exposure. Instructor/Academy travel now also avoids enemy pressure and checks the actual end-turn radius-2 danger. A General starting from safety will not deliberately end on a dangerous travel tile, while a General already trapped in danger may use a nonzero-danger path only when its end-turn plot is strictly safer than its current plot, avoiding a safety rule that would itself pin the unit in a collapsing city.
- **Fixed Base AdvCiv issue - zero-turn unsafe-city retreat trap:** the K-Mod-derived `AI_retreatToCity` could let a threatened defenseless land unit choose its current unsafe city as the best retreat destination. Its path length is zero, so it could beat every genuine escape city and return `MISSION_SKIP`. AdvCiv-SAS now excludes a threatened non-defender's current city while searching for a retreat destination; if no real alternative exists, the existing fallback remains unchanged and can still leave the unit there rather than manufacturing an impossible escape.
- **Improved SAS Great General policy - era-tunable Military Instructor-first behavior:** Base AdvCiv can attach a threatened Great General to a combat unit before the normal Academy/Instructor sequence. AdvCiv-SAS deliberately gates weak attachments very heavily because Military Instructors are currently preferred for balance. `SAS_GREAT_GENERAL_AS_MILITARY_INSTRUCTOR_PREFER_FIRST_THROUGH_ERA` now makes the additional Instructor-first priority tunable: `-1` disables it, nonnegative values apply it through the corresponding era index, and the dynamically resolved `ERA_FUTURE` index or higher applies it in all eras. The ordinary Academy, attachment, retreat and safety fallbacks remain available when a suitable Instructor action cannot be made. A later autoplay exposed one narrow consistency gap: Portugal's General `1777738` was already standing in Guimarães on turn 277 with `citySafe=1` and `currentPlotDangerR2=2`; `AI_join` rejected the city for radius-2 danger, then the very next Great-General decision selected `AI_construct(1)` and SASGameRecord recorded a Military Academy in that same city. Because both Instructor joining and Academy construction consume the General immediately when it is already on the city plot, only the Instructor was being blocked by a travel-oriented danger gate despite having no travel exposure. `AI_join` now allows that immediate current-city join while keeping the radius-2 danger rejection for destinations that require travel.
- **Improved Great General death reporting and Timeline persistence:** Base AdvCiv passed `getNameKey()` to Great General death notifications, so a named casualty could show only its personal name and hide whether it was the free General or e.g. a named Longbowman carrying one. AdvCiv-SAS now uses `getReplayName()` for these messages so unit type and personal name stay together. Player-caused Great General deaths are also persisted as replay major events, allowing the Info Screen Timeline to display them instead of leaving the event only in the transient top-center message stream.
- **Improved SASGameRecord/BBAI observability:** a defenseless Great Person destroyed directly through a player-caused `CvUnit::kill` path could bypass the existing combat-result record. That player-kill path now records the death without duplicating ordinary combat rows. Great-Person birth rows also record the newborn `unitId` and spawn coordinates, while dedicated BBAI Great General level-3 diagnostics record candidate rejection reasons and numeric current/city/path-end danger. This allows one General to be followed from birth through AI decisions to Instructor/Academy/attachment/death outcome.
- **Post-fix autoplay validation:** a 457-turn test with only Great General BBAI diagnostics enabled produced 91 Great General births, 90 Military Instructor joins, no Academy/attachment outcomes and 1 free-General death. 75 of the 90 successful Generals joined on their birth turn, 12 one turn later and 3 two turns later; 41 settled in a city other than their birth city. All 6 Generals whose first AI decision began with radius-2 danger above zero successfully reached an Instructor outcome, including starts at danger 22 and 28. The sole death was qualitatively different and appears unavoidable by the AI movement fixes: Russia's General `1114142` was born in Rostov on turn 362 and killed there during Rostov's capture on the same turn, after Moscow had already fallen earlier that turn. Rostov was therefore Russia's only remaining city, the safe-birth-city selector had no alternative, and BBAI contains no Great General move for the unit because it died before Russia received an AI turn.

This remains a mixed issue rather than one Civ4 bug or one SAS regression. The unsafe birth-city selector, inverted Academy safety test and zero-turn retreat trap are concrete behaviors present in Base AdvCiv; travel protection and death/replay reporting are inherited behavior hardened in SAS; Instructor-first use and near-disabled weak attachments are deliberate SAS balance policy; and the missing direct-kill row was a SASGameRecord instrumentation gap. No claim is made that the AdvCiv-specific defects are also present in unmodified Civilization IV: Beyond the Sword, which was not the comparison target of this investigation.

Fixed/improved and documented with the help of ChatGPT-5.6-Sol thanks.

<a id="ki-205"></a>

## KI#205 - (Fixed/Improved) Major K-Mod World-Wonder focus refactor bug rejected the AI's best production cities, while an AdvCiv-SAS game-speed regression could almost disable cheap-Wonder catch-up on slow speeds

Screenshots/files for this issue: [google drive folder link](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/17qDbSL6xRE-NA4KgIs7sdexsgZv6uS9y?usp=sharing).

[A player had previously reported](https://forums.civfanatics.com/threads/advciv-sas-simple-advanced-strategy.699716/post-16971507) that the AI seemed not to build ordinary World Wonders, especially on a slow game speed. That report predated many later AdvCiv-SAS balance changes and initially looked likely to be obsolete because recent Normal-speed autoplays do build and contest many World Wonders. A fresh Huge Donut / Slow-speed autoplay nevertheless reproduced the concern dramatically: through turn 601 with 16 players, SASGameRecord in save file 477 (Huge, Donut, Slow) contained 11 `WONDER_BUILT` rows by T601 (1406 AD), but these were only 4 religious shrines, 6 Heroic Epics and 1 National Epic. No ordinary World Wonder was completed. The Info Screen likewise showed only the four shrines in the World Wonders table.

The investigation found two independent World-Wonder AI defects:

- **Fixed AdvCiv-SAS game-speed regression in the cheap-Wonder catch-up gate:** `CvCityAI::AI_buildingValue` compares `getProductionNeeded(eBuilding)` against era-based `SAS_AI_BUILDING_VALUE_WORLD_WONDERS_CHEAP_ICOST_CAP_*_NORMAL` thresholds. The cost returned by `getProductionNeeded` is not raw XML cost: `CvPlayer::getProductionNeeded(BuildingTypes)` multiplies building cost by the current game speed's `ConstructPercent` (along with the existing start-era/handicap adjustments). The cap therefore has to be scaled by the same game-speed factor to preserve the intended Normal-speed threshold. AdvCiv-SAS practical commit 5203 (`8a13288983`) originally implemented this correctly through `iCheapWWCapAdjusted = iCheapWWCapNormal * iGameSpeedMultiplier / 100`. Practical commit 5477 (`b33174f828`) later removed that scaling during a broader raw-XML-cost cleanup and changed the nearby comment to say that `iCost` was game-speed-independent XML cost. That assumption was incorrect for this code path. On Slow speed (300% construct cost), the AI's effective cheap-Wonder threshold became roughly one third of its intended relative value; faster speeds were skewed in the opposite direction. The original game-speed scaling is now restored. Normal-speed behavior is unchanged by this correction.

- **Fixed inherited K-Mod World-Wonder focus inversion:** when `BUILDINGFOCUS_WORLDWONDER` is explicitly requested, current inherited code rejected the candidate whenever `iProductionRank <= 3`. Production rank 1 is the best production city, so this excluded the AI's three strongest hammer cities. The recently included full K-Mod commit history makes the origin unusually clear. Before K-Mod commit 1030 (`418581f6bd`), the corresponding World-Wonder logic positively accepted/boosted a candidate when `findBaseYieldRateRank(YIELD_PRODUCTION) <= 3`. Commit 1030 refactored that check out of the large evaluation loop and into an early veto, describing it as essentially the same original check moved earlier, but retained the same `<= 3` comparison underneath `return 0`. Moving a positive condition into a rejection gate required reversing the comparison; failing to do so inverted the behavior. AdvCiv-SAS now rejects `iProductionRank > 3` instead, restoring the intended top-three-production-city eligibility.

These two defects could reinforce each other. AdvCiv-SAS deliberately makes early World Wonders less attractive than Base AdvCiv in order to avoid wasting scarce early production and reduce easy human Wonder exploitation; its era-based cheap-Wonder rule is the intended catch-up path that lets old inexpensive Wonders become attractive later. The game-speed regression could effectively remove that catch-up path on Slow/Very Slow speeds, while the inherited K-Mod focus inversion could simultaneously prevent explicit World-Wonder searches from using the cities best equipped to build them. This explains why increasing generic Wonder desire or weakening the SAS optimization would have been the wrong first response: there were concrete correctness issues underneath the balance policy.

This investigation also provided a practical validation of the recently expanded AdvCiv-SAS light-source handoff. `commit_diffs` folder includes filtered textual patches for the full current-HEAD ancestry across K-Mod, pre-SAS AdvCiv and the later SAS branch history. Using those shared commit diffs bundled in the light-source ZIP, ChatGPT-5.6-Sol could trace the SAS game-speed regression from its correct introduction in commit 5203 to the incorrect refactor in commit 5477, and independently compare K-Mod 1030's pre/post-refactor World-Wonder condition without requiring live Git access or GitHub. The history therefore supplied not just commit messages but the exact old code needed to distinguish a balance choice from a regression and an inherited refactor bug.

The combined fix was then validated with another Huge Donut / Slow-speed autoplay through turn 601 (`SASGameRecord_20260818T193115Z_load1.log`). The completed-Wonder result already gives a clear before/after: the pre-fix run (`SASGameRecord_20260818T184659Z_new1.log`) had zero ordinary World Wonders, while the post-fix log has 17 `WONDER_BUILT` rows consisting of 4 religious shrines, 6 Heroic/National Epics and 7 ordinary World Wonders: Stonehenge (England), Pyramids and Colossus (Kingdom of Benin), Great Wall and Great Lighthouse (Egypt), Statue of Zeus (Arabia), and Great Library (Egypt). The periodic city snapshots make the recovery even clearer: at turn 600 the pre-fix log had zero cities with `productionKind=WONDER`, while the post-fix log had 15 ordinary World-Wonder builds active across 9 civilizations (9 Parthenons and 6 Temples of Kukulkan), plus 1 Heroic Epic. This is strong confirmation that the AI World-Wonder selection path itself is functioning again on Slow speed rather than a few Wonders merely completing by chance. The two corrections remain conceptually separable: the game-speed fix leaves Normal-speed thresholds unchanged, while the K-Mod production-rank fix restores intended World-Wonder focus behavior on all speeds.

Fixed/improved, validated in a repeat Slow/Donut autoplay, and documented with the help of ChatGPT-5.6-Sol thanks.

## KI#206 - (Fixed K-Mod bug) AI random-event building-change valuation missed percent normalization, making building creation or destruction worth 100 times the intended production-cost component

A systematic current-tree audit of raw XML `iCost` / `getProductionCost()` uses was started after KI#205 exposed a game-speed regression caused by confusing raw XML cost with `getProductionNeeded`. Most current raw production-cost uses are intentional: they are buildability sentinels, tactical/relative cost proxies, drafting formulas defined directly from XML cost, explicit SAS XML-cost gates, logging/UI values, or ratios where applying the common game-speed production multiplier would either cancel out or incorrectly make tactical behavior depend on game speed.

The audit nevertheless found a separate definite arithmetic error in `CvPlayerAI::AI_eventValue`. The unit-event valuation path converts raw unit production cost to the current game speed by multiplying by `TrainPercent` and then dividing by 100. The analogous building-event path multiplied raw building production cost by `ConstructPercent` but never divided by 100.

For example, before the fix a positive building-value component of 200 raw units became `200 * 100 = 20,000` on Normal speed rather than remaining 200, and became `200 * 300 = 60,000` on Slow rather than the intended 600. The error was therefore a constant 100x overvaluation after the intended game-speed scaling, not merely a Slow-speed imbalance.

This affects real random-event outcomes in the current XML with nonzero `iBuildingChange`, including events that create or destroy Forges, Theatres, Factories, Military Academies, Academies, Hydro Plants and Broadcast Towers. Depending on the sign of the building change, the inflated term could make the AI grossly overvalue receiving a building or grossly over-penalize losing one relative to the event's other effects.

The fix simply adds the missing `iBuildingValue /= 100` immediately after applying `ConstructPercent`, matching the already-correct unit-event calculation. This changes only AI event-option valuation; it does not alter actual building production costs or event effects.

The lineage check confirms that this is not an AdvCiv-SAS regression. The same missing normalization is present in Base AdvCiv 1.14. The light-source history also shows it already in K-Mod practical commit 3 (`2414225e64`, the initial source-bearing K-Mod commit from 27 December 2010), where `AI_eventValue` multiplies both unit and building production values by the corresponding game-speed percentages without dividing by 100. More revealingly, K-Mod practical commit 478 (`bfc3c3cca7`, "Added some missing components to the AI's evaluation of event options.") added the missing `/= 100` to both unit-event paths but left the analogous building-event path unchanged. No later K-Mod or Base AdvCiv change corrected that building branch, and it remains present in AdvCiv 1.14.

KI#206 is therefore classified as an inherited K-Mod/Base AdvCiv bug, not an SAS-specific issue. K-Mod practical 478 is not claimed as the origin: it is the especially useful historical point where K-Mod corrected the two adjacent unit-event normalization paths but missed the building path. The bug is already present in practical 3, the first source-bearing K-Mod commit available in this repository history. The available history does not establish whether K-Mod originally introduced the omission or inherited it from BtS/BBAI before that boundary, so no stronger pre-K-Mod origin claim is made.

ChatGPT-5.6-Sol found the defect while locally auditing current-tree XML/raw-cost semantics after KI#205, rather than during the later systematic historical sweep. The Base AdvCiv 1.14 source supplied alongside the SAS source confirmed that the bug is pre-SAS, and ChatGPT-5.6-Sol then traced the K-Mod lineage entirely from the light-source ZIP's shared `commit_diffs` folder corpus, without needing an Internet lookup. This is the same kind of local Git-history archaeology that proved useful for KI#205 and motivated keeping a resumable archaeology suite.

Fixed and lineage-traced with the help of ChatGPT-5.6-Sol thanks.

## KI#207 - (Fixed Base AdvCiv bug) UWAI random team-member selection mixed 0-based random indexes with iterator positions, biasing the first member and excluding the last

The systematic AdvCiv/K-Mod history archaeology found its first previously-unfixed surviving defect while reviewing AdvCivPreSAS newest to oldest. AdvCiv practical 2945 (`f016996eb6`, "Let UWAI negotiate with a random team member") introduced `CvTeam::getRandomMemberAlive`, allowing UWAI war-related diplomacy to choose a random living player from a team rather than always using the team leader. The intended change is useful for team games, but its selection logic mixed two incompatible index conventions.

`SyncRandNum(iValid)` returns a zero-based random value in `[0, iValid)`. The old loop compared that value against `MemberIter::nextIndex()`, whose documented `ListIterator.nextIndex` semantics describe the position of the element that would be returned next. For the first currently yielded member, `nextIndex()` is therefore already 1 rather than 0. With three eligible AI members, random indexes 0 and 1 both selected the first member, index 2 selected the second, and the third member could never be selected. A two-member AI team degenerated to 100% selection of the first member and 0% of the second.

The human-only branch had an additional mismatch. `iValid` counts only human team members, but the old comparison used `MemberIter::nextIndex()`, which advances across all living members. On a mixed human/AI team, the random value and iterator position therefore did not even refer to the same eligible-member sequence, making selection depend incorrectly on the placement of ineligible AI members.

This matters in real UWAI diplomacy paths that still call `getRandomMemberAlive`, including selecting representatives for peace negotiations, attempts to find a new master/vassal agreement, human contacts, and attempts to amend tensions before war. Ordinary one-player-per-team games are unaffected because there is only one eligible member, which likely helped the defect survive unnoticed; team games and Permanent Alliance situations can use multiple members and therefore expose the bias.

The fix preserves the synchronized RNG consumption and the original eligible count, but replaces the iterator-position comparison with an explicit zero-based counter that advances only for eligible members. The selected representative is therefore uniformly distributed across exactly the same set counted by `iValid`; no extra random calls are added.

The lineage is unusually clear. Practical 2945 introduced the faulty comparison directly. Later AdvCiv practical 3209 changed the RNG helper from `getSRandNum` to `SyncRandNum` but left the index comparison intact, and the bug survived into Base AdvCiv and AdvCiv-SAS. The iterator's `nextIndex()` semantics predate practical 2945, so this is not a later iterator refactor breaking formerly correct code.

This was the first **previously-unfixed** defect found by the systematic historical sweep itself. The sweep started at AdvCivPreSAS practical 4343 and reached practical 2945 after reviewing 1,399 historical commits. It did encounter a genuine historical defect earlier at practical 3956 (`da462d23f0`), the `ExtraFreeOutsideUnits` default bug, but AdvCiv-SAS had already independently fixed and documented that issue as KI#92. Other suspicious candidates were rejected after tracing their semantics rather than being counted as findings. KI#205 and KI#206 were targeted lineage traces/current-tree discoveries made before the systematic sweep and are therefore not counted as its first hit.

Found through the systematic AdvCiv/K-Mod archaeology, fixed and documented with the help of ChatGPT-5.6-Sol thanks.

<a id="ki-208"></a>

## KI#208 - (Fixed Base AdvCiv bug) Worst-enemy trade-memory optimization could forget a required recalculation when later teams overwrote its flag

The systematic AdvCiv/K-Mod history archaeology found its second previously-unfixed surviving defect at AdvCiv practical 2833 (`98b7a50fac`, "Minor optimization in update of worst enemy"). The affected code is in `CvTeamAI::AI_updateWorstEnemy`, where AdvCiv first selects a tentative new worst enemy and then decays old enemy-trade/grant memories before committing that choice.

That memory decay can itself change attitudes. In particular, if the tentative new worst enemy had previously traded with the old worst enemy, reducing its `EnemyPeacetimeGrantValue` or `EnemyPeacetimeTradeValue` improves relations with that tentative enemy. The first worst-enemy calculation can therefore become stale, so AdvCiv practical 2833 added `bUpdateWorstEnemyAgain` to rerun the selection only when the tentative new worst enemy was one of the teams whose memories were changed. The optimization is sensible; the flag implementation was not.

The old loop assigned `bUpdateWorstEnemyAgain = (eOther == eBestTeam)` for every team with nonzero relevant memory. This made the flag non-sticky. If the tentative new worst enemy was encountered first, the flag became `true`, but any later unrelated team with nonzero memory immediately assigned it back to `false`. Whether the required second worst-enemy calculation happened therefore depended on team iteration order. For example, if team B was the tentative new worst enemy and its memories were decayed, then team C was processed afterward, B could improve enough not to remain the true worst enemy while C nevertheless cleared the recalculation flag.

A later non-best team becoming less disliked cannot create this particular need for a rerun: it was already not the maximum-enmity candidate and the decay only improves relations with it. The important state is therefore simply whether the tentative `eBestTeam` was modified at any point during the loop. Once that has happened, later teams must not erase the fact.

The fix keeps practical 2833's optimization but makes the flag sticky: when `eOther == eBestTeam`, set `bUpdateWorstEnemyAgain = true`; otherwise leave its existing value untouched. No extra loop, RNG, or attitude calculation is added unless the original optimization already intended the second pass. This prevents `m_eWorstEnemy` from being committed from a stale first calculation merely because another team's memory happened to be processed later.

The lineage is direct. Practical 2833 introduced the faulty assignment on its development branch, and AdvCiv practical 2998 (`8c36049d43`, "Merge branch 0.99 into master") carried the same code into master. No later historical patch corrected the assignment, and the exact logic survived into Base AdvCiv and AdvCiv-SAS until this archaeology pass. In gameplay, the stale worst-enemy state can temporarily affect diplomacy and any logic that reads the team's worst enemy until a later update happens to correct it; the bug does not require or imply permanent save corruption.

This is the systematic sweep's second previously-unfixed surviving defect, after KI#207 at practical 2945. The sweep reviewed practical 2944 down through 2833 carefully before stopping here; suspicious-looking changes that did not survive semantic/current-code checks were not counted as findings.

Found through the systematic AdvCiv/K-Mod archaeology, fixed and documented with the help of ChatGPT-5.6-Sol thanks.

<a id="ki-209"></a>

## KI#209 - (Fixed Base AdvCiv bug) Player reassignment saved random-leader status from the random-civilization flag, corrupting independent setup state

The systematic AdvCiv/K-Mod history archaeology found its third previously-unfixed surviving defect at AdvCiv practical 2532 (`60a15e6434`, "Handle assignment of random civs and leaders in the DLL"). The affected code is `CvInitCore::reassignPlayer`, which temporarily saves the target player slot's setup state, copies another player's state into that slot, and then restores the saved target state into the displaced slot.

Practical 2532 added separate bookkeeping for whether a civilization and leader had originally been chosen randomly, but the save step contained a direct copy/paste error:

```cpp
bool bRandomCiv = m_abCivChosenRandomly.get(eNewID);
bool bRandomLeader = m_abCivChosenRandomly.get(eNewID);
```

The second line reads the civilization-randomness map again instead of `m_abLeaderChosenRandomly`. Later in the same function, `bRandomLeader` is restored through `m_abLeaderChosenRandomly.set(eOldID, bRandomLeader)`, so a reassigned slot whose civilization and leader randomness differ has its saved leader provenance incorrectly forced to equal its civilization provenance.

For example, a manually chosen civilization with a randomly chosen leader has the intended state `randomCiv=false, randomLeader=true`; the old save step turned that into `false, false`. Conversely, a random civilization paired with a manually chosen leader can become `true, true`. Ordinary games where civilization and leader randomness naturally move together can mask the mistake, which helps explain why the typo survived. The distinction matters when those choices are independent, notably with Unrestricted Leaders (`GAMEOPTION_LEAD_ANY_CIV`) or other setup states where only one of the two was randomized.

The bookkeeping is not merely descriptive. `CvInitCore::wasLeaderRandomlyChosen` reads `m_abLeaderChosenRandomly` whenever the civilization-randomness shortcut does not apply, and the result is used by setup synchronization/re-randomization logic such as `setLeaderExternal` and `reRandomizeCivsAndLeaders`. Corrupting the flag can therefore make later setup handling misclassify whether a leader was actually randomized.

The fix is deliberately surgical: save `bRandomLeader` from `m_abLeaderChosenRandomly.get(eNewID)`. Civilization and leader random-choice state are then preserved independently, exactly as the paired restore assignments already imply. No RNG or assignment policy changes.

The lineage is direct. Practical 2532 introduced the incorrect member access in the same patch that added the random civilization/leader bookkeeping to `reassignPlayer`; no later historical correction was found, and the exact line survived into Base AdvCiv and AdvCiv-SAS until this archaeology pass.

This is the systematic sweep's third previously-unfixed surviving defect, after KI#207 at practical 2945 and KI#208 at practical 2833. From practical 2832 down through 2532, 365 additional unique historical commit SHAs were reviewed before stopping here; suspicious-looking changes that did not survive semantic/current-code checks were not counted as findings.

Found through the systematic AdvCiv/K-Mod archaeology, fixed and documented with the help of ChatGPT-5.6-Sol thanks.

<a id="ki-210"></a>

## KI#210 - (Fixed Base AdvCiv bug) Vote-selection iterator refactor could pair a voting team with itself, creating bogus self first-contact state

The systematic AdvCiv/K-Mod history archaeology found its fourth previously-unfixed surviving defect at AdvCiv practical 2502 (`cbc25c22bd`, "Misc. refactoring"). The affected code is `CvGame::doVoteSelection`, which makes voting members of an active Apostolic Palace or United Nations vote source meet one another before the vote-selection logic continues.

Before practical 2502, the two team loops used numeric indexes and deliberately started the second loop at `iTeam2 = iTeam1 + 1`. That encoded two useful invariants at once: a team could never be paired with itself, and each unordered team pair was considered only once. Practical 2502 replaced both numeric loops with `TeamIter<MAJOR_CIV>`, but the inner iterator starts from the beginning for every outer team and no equivalent self-exclusion was added. The refactor therefore allowed `itTeam1` and `itTeam2` to refer to the same voting team.

This is not harmlessly rejected before state changes. At this point in AdvCiv history, `isHasMet` uses `m_aiHasMetTurn` with an initial value of `-1`, so a team does not begin by counting itself as already met. `doVoteSelection` can therefore call `meet` with the same team on both sides. `CvTeam::makeHasMet` does contain an `eOther == getID()` guard, but that check occurs only after `makeHasSeen`, setting `m_aiHasMetTurn`, `updateTechShare`, and the Python `firstContact` event. Thus the late guard prevents the later ordinary-contact handling but does not prevent the bogus self-contact state/event that already happened. Current AdvCiv-SAS instrumentation could also observe such a call as a self team-meeting record when detailed game-record logging is enabled.

The practical effect is narrower than an ordinary foreign first contact and should not be overstated. Many higher-level team/diplomacy iterators explicitly exclude the same team, so this does not by itself imply broad AI diplomatic corruption. The definite problem is that an AP/UN voting-member pass can mark a team as having seen/met itself and emit a first-contact event for the same team; any less-defensive consumer of that raw state/event can then observe something that should never have existed.

The fix restores the lost caller invariant directly. The inner voting-member loop now skips `itTeam2` when its team ID equals `itTeam1` before attempting any contact. No generic `CvTeam::meet` behavior, vote eligibility, RNG, or ordinary foreign-team contact is changed. Processing foreign pairs twice after the iterator refactor remains harmless here because the first pass establishes contact and the reverse pass then sees `isHasMet` already true.

The lineage is direct. Practical 2502 changed `for (int iTeam2 = iTeam1 + 1; ...)` to a fresh full `TeamIter<MAJOR_CIV>` and simultaneously converted the contact calls to iterator form; no replacement self-check appeared in that patch. No later historical correction was found, and the same loop survived into Base AdvCiv and AdvCiv-SAS until this archaeology pass.

This is the systematic sweep's fourth previously-unfixed surviving defect, after KI#207 at practical 2945, KI#208 at practical 2833, and KI#209 at practical 2532. From practical 2531 down through 2502, 30 additional unique historical commit SHAs were reviewed before stopping here. Suspicious historical changes that were already fixed later or did not survive semantic/current-code checks were not counted as findings.

Found through the systematic AdvCiv/K-Mod archaeology, fixed and documented with the help of ChatGPT-5.6-Sol thanks.

<a id="ki-211"></a>

## KI#211 - (Fixed inherited K-Mod/Base AdvCiv bug) Terrain attack bonuses were reversed in AI attacker-strength estimates against unknown defenders

The systematic AdvCiv/K-Mod history archaeology found its fifth previously-unfixed surviving defect, and the first one found after the sweep entered the K-Mod segment, while giving K-Mod practical 3 (`2414225e64`, the initial source-bearing K-Mod commit from 27 December 2010) its own deep audit. The affected code is the special `CvUnit::maxCombatStr` mode used when the attacking unit is known but the defender is not: callers pass the attacking unit itself as `pAttacker`, which makes `maxCombatStr` estimate that attacker's strength on the target plot without requiring a particular defender.

The function handles that special case by calculating the attacker's plot-dependent attack modifiers in the same sign convention used when evaluating a defender against a known attacker, accumulating them in `iTempModifier`, and then reversing the subtotal at the end. City, hills and feature attack bonuses all follow that pattern. For example, a +20% hills attack bonus first contributes `-20` to `iTempModifier`; ordinary known-defender evaluation adds that negative subtotal to the defender-side strength calculation, while unknown-defender attacker evaluation instead executes `iModifier -= iTempModifier`, turning the same `-20` back into the intended +20% attacker-strength bonus.

The terrain-attack branch was the lone exception:

```cpp
iExtraModifier = -pAttacker->terrainAttackModifier(pAttackedPlot->getTerrainType());
iModifier += iExtraModifier;
```

Because it added the negative terrain-attack value directly to `iModifier` instead of the reversible `iTempModifier` subtotal, the later `iModifier -= iTempModifier` could not reverse it. A positive terrain attack bonus could therefore become a penalty in this particular AI strength estimate. In a simplified case with no other modifiers, +20% terrain attack should give an estimated 120% of base strength; the buggy branch instead leaves `iModifier=-20`, which follows the negative-modifier formula and yields roughly `10000 / 120 = 83.3%` of base strength before the later effective-strength adjustments. This is not merely omitting the bonus: it changes its sign.

The defect does not mean ordinary known-attacker/known-defender combat calculation is generally reversed. In that normal configuration, the negative attacker modifier is supposed to be applied to the defender-side calculation, and moving the terrain term into `iTempModifier` preserves that result because the function normally finishes with `iModifier += iTempModifier`. The bug is specifically the attacker-known/defender-unknown mode, where the temporary attacker subtotal is deliberately subtracted instead.

That special mode is live AI code, not a dormant or diagnostic-only helper. Current `CvSelectionGroupAI::AI_sumStrength` calls `AI_currEffectiveStr(pAttackedPlot, pUnit, ...)`, deliberately passing the unit itself as the `pOther`/attacker argument and thereby reaching `pAttacker == this` in `maxCombatStr`. `GroupPathFinder` then uses `AI_sumStrength(&kTo)` when computing the attack ratio and path cost for defended plots, and `CvPlayerAI::AI_cityTargetStrengthByPath` adds `AI_sumStrength(pCity->plot())` when estimating how much attacking strength can reach a city. AdvCiv-SAS's newer low-power attacker ordering also calls `AI_currEffectiveStr(pPlot, &kLoopUnit, ...)` in the same special mode. The incorrect terrain term can therefore affect live AI strength comparisons, pathing/target-strength estimates and SAS attack ordering rather than only an informational display.

The current XML makes the path relevant in practice. The archaeology audit counted 30 current unit types with nonzero terrain-attack modifiers, including multiple +20% examples such as the Dog Soldier on Plains, Roman Legionary on Plains, War Chariot on Desert, Numidian Cavalry on Plains, Greek Hoplite on Plains and Babylonian Bowman on Desert. AdvCiv-SAS also deliberately allows terrain attack modifiers to matter in city combat, so city-target estimates are not automatically insulated from the problem merely because a target plot contains a city.

The historical boundary is clear but the pre-K-Mod authorship is not. The exact asymmetric terrain line is already present in K-Mod practical 3, the first source-bearing K-Mod snapshot available in this repository history. AdvCiv practical 1733 (`0d648df6db`) later touched and preserved the same block without changing the direct `iModifier += iExtraModifier`, and no later correcting patch was found before the line reached current AdvCiv-SAS. Because practical 3 is an initial source snapshot rather than the beginning of every line's ancestry, the available history does not establish whether K-Mod itself introduced the mistake or inherited it from BtS/BBAI/Unofficial Patch ancestry. KI#211 is therefore classified conservatively as an inherited K-Mod/Base AdvCiv bug present at the earliest available K-Mod source boundary, not claimed as a proven K-Mod-authored regression.

The repair is deliberately one-line in behavior: after calculating the negative terrain attack modifier, accumulate it in `iTempModifier` just like city, hills and feature attack modifiers. A short SAS comment documents why this otherwise easy-to-miss accumulator choice matters. For an ordinary known defender, `iTempModifier` is still added and the result is unchanged. For an unknown defender, the existing subtraction now reverses the terrain term together with its sibling attack modifiers, restoring the intended positive contribution. No XML, combat rule, RNG, ordinary combat-odds formula or unit balance value is changed.

The surrounding practical-3 audit was intentionally not declared complete merely because this defect was found. Before stopping at KI#211, the sweep had also re-proved the old `iIncome` divisor candidate safe, found several genuine historical K-Mod mistakes that were later repaired, and performed a brace-aware audit of 903 assertion/bounds checks that reduced an apparent cluster of mismatches to one already-superseded debug assertion. Subsequent dedicated passes completed and certified practical 3 before the archaeology continued through practical 2 and 1.

Found through the systematic AdvCiv/K-Mod archaeology, fixed and documented with the help of ChatGPT-5.6-Sol thanks.

<a id="ki-212"></a>

## KI#212 - (Fixed minor inherited K-Mod/Base AdvCiv bug) AI Barbarian attacker CombatDetails were written to the defender-barbarian field

The continuing deep audit of K-Mod practical 3 (`2414225e64`, the initial source-bearing K-Mod snapshot) found a second surviving defect in the same `CvUnit::maxCombatStr` combat-details plumbing as KI#211. This one is deliberately classified as minor: the combat-strength arithmetic is correct, and the current built-in combat log happens to mask the wrong field assignment, but the `CombatDetails` structure exposed to Python reports the attacker/defender side incorrectly for one AI-versus-Barbarian case.

`CombatDetails` carries separate fields for Barbarian modifiers on the unit being evaluated (`...TB`, interpreted by AdvCiv's own struct comment as “This is Barbarian”) and on the attacking unit (`...AB`, “Attacker is Barbarian”). The ordinary human-handicap paths respect that split: when the defender itself is Barbarian, `iBarbarianCombatModifierTB` is populated; when the attacker is Barbarian, `iBarbarianCombatModifierAB` is populated. The corresponding AI fields are likewise separately declared and exported to Python as `iAIBarbarianCombatModifierTB` and `iAIBarbarianCombatModifierAB`.

The AI-attacker branch contained a copy/paste mismatch. When `pAttacker->isBarbarian()` is true and the defender is AI-controlled, the function correctly computes the AI-vs-Barbarian modifier and applies it to `iModifier`, but then stored the reporting value in the defender-side field:

```cpp
pCombatDetails->iAIBarbarianCombatModifierTB = iExtraModifier;
```

The semantically corresponding attacker-side field `iAIBarbarianCombatModifierAB` is reset to zero with the rest of `CombatDetails`, exported through `CyStructsInterface1.cpp`, and read by Python, but current `maxCombatStr` never assigned it. Meanwhile `...TB` was assigned by both the genuine defender-Barbarian AI branch and this attacker-Barbarian AI branch. The exposed data contract therefore could not distinguish the two cases even though the structure explicitly provides separate fields for them.

The current built-in combat log makes the defect easy to miss. `Assets/Python/CvUtil.py::combatDetailMessageBuilder` reads both `iAIBarbarianCombatModifierTB` and `iAIBarbarianCombatModifierAB` using the same `TXT_KEY_COMBAT_MESSAGE_BARBARIAN_AI_COMBAT` text key and the same sign handling. Consequently, moving the value from the wrong TB field to the correct AB field does not change the ordinary visible combat-log line. The underlying strength calculation also never depended on the `CombatDetails` field: it had already added the same `iExtraModifier` to `iModifier`. The definite impact is therefore semantic/API correctness for Python or other consumers that inspect the fields separately, rather than changed combat odds or current AI behavior.

The faulty assignment is already present in K-Mod practical 3 and was preserved through later K-Mod/AdvCiv edits of the same block, including AdvCiv practical 2662 and the later formatting/Barbarian-combat changes that still retained the same `...TB` write. It survives in current AdvCiv-SAS. As with KI#211, practical 3 is an initial source snapshot rather than proof of line authorship, so the available history establishes that the defect is inherited from the earliest available K-Mod source boundary but does not establish whether K-Mod itself introduced it or inherited it from earlier BtS/BBAI/Unofficial Patch ancestry.

The repair changes only that reporting assignment to `iAIBarbarianCombatModifierAB`, with a short SAS comment identifying the inherited AB/TB copy/paste. No strength arithmetic, handicap value, RNG, combat rule, text key or balance parameter changes. The built-in combat log remains visually equivalent, while the exported `CombatDetails` fields now match their documented attacker/defender semantics.

Finding KI#212 did not by itself certify practical 3 or advance the historical commit counter. Subsequent dedicated reverse-fix, serialization and sibling-field passes completed the audit and certified practical 3 before the archaeology continued through practical 2 and 1.

Found through the systematic AdvCiv/K-Mod archaeology, fixed and documented with the help of ChatGPT-5.6-Sol thanks.

## KI#213 - (Pending Architectural, broadened by current-tree audit) Split city/Worker best-build policies hide valid custom land jobs from AI planning

The systematic AdvCiv-SAS archaeology found that Worker demand and actual Worker job selection can disagree because they consult different build policies. SAS deliberately disables ordinary land results in the legacy city-side `CvCityAI::AI_getBestBuild` cache and instead lets the extensively customized `CvUnitAI::AI_bestCityBuild` choose land improvements. `CvCityAI::AI_updateWorkersHaveAndNeeded`, however, still uses the legacy cache when deciding whether some plots represent valid Worker demand.

A concrete surviving case is a worked, unimproved Flood Plains plot without a bonus. `AI_bestCityBuild` explicitly gives this plot a valid Cottage, or a Cottage/Farm choice under low-food pressure. Because Flood Plains are a Feature and the legacy best-build cache remains empty, `AI_updateWorkersHaveAndNeeded` classifies the plot as worked but unimprovable rather than as a current Worker job. The city can therefore understate Worker demand even though an actual Worker would recognize useful work there.

The C031-WIP318 current-tree audit broadened the consequences beyond the demand count itself. The false zero can suppress Worker production through `CvCityAI::AI_chooseUnit`, reject Worker transport or unloading into the area, and classify existing Workers for completed-area evacuation even while the custom land evaluator still sees useful work. Other consumers of the split city-side policy include good-plot counts, target population, food-kept valuation, empire splitting, poor-worked-plot counts and City Site Evaluator protection, so repairing individual callers would leave the same architectural disagreement elsewhere.

The pending repair should address the architectural split rather than hardcode Flood Plains or add another approximate feature test. Extract the city/plot build-policy evaluation from `CvUnitAI::AI_bestCityBuild` into shared city/player-side logic, let both the city best-build cache/demand users and Worker selection consume that policy, and keep unit-specific legality, pathfinding, reservations, grouping and mission execution in `CvUnitAI`. This is intentionally deferred to its own implementation, compile and autoplay-validation commit because the customized Worker system is large and historically fragile.

Found and documented through the systematic AdvCiv-SAS archaeology with the help of ChatGPT-5.6-Sol; implementation remains pending.

## KI#214 - (Fixed AdvCiv-SAS bug) Irrigation-chain constrained search could discard the only route that satisfied the plot limit

The deterministic SAS irrigation-chain search minimizes overwrite cost while imposing a separate maximum number of route plots. Its previous state stored only one best cost for each plot. Cost and route length are independent dimensions, so a cheap longer route could overwrite and discard a more expensive shorter route to the same plot even when only the shorter state could reach irrigation within the configured plot limit.

For example, one route can reach an intermediate plot in 2 steps with roughly 2550 overwrite cost while another reaches it in 7 empty-plot steps with roughly 2100 cost. The old search retained only the cheaper 7-step state. If irrigation was another 6 plots away, that retained route needed 13 plots and was rejected by a 12-plot limit, while the discarded 2-step state would have completed the valid chain in 8 plots. The AI could therefore report no irrigation chain despite a valid one existing within the limit.

The fix makes route length part of the search state. Instead of one best cost per plot, the search now retains one best cost for every `(plot, steps)` state through the configured maximum. The priority queue still selects the least-cost admissible route, but a cheaper state reached in 7 steps no longer erases a separate 2-step state at the same plot. With the default 12-plot limit this uses 13 bounded states per map plot; the existing generation stamps continue to initialize only states reached by each repeated Worker-city search.

The defect was introduced with the deterministic irrigation-chain search in AdvCiv-SAS practical 6076 (`2cc4ccaf5d`). The repair does not change connector eligibility, overwrite penalties, route valuation, the maximum plot limit or Worker mission execution. The diagnostic count is renamed from visited plots to visited states because the corrected search can evaluate the same plot at several route lengths.

Save file 478 provided a full compiled-DLL validation on a Huge Pangaea map. SASGameRecord confirmed that 501 autoplay turns were requested and the game completed normally with a Space Race victory on turn 497, while its performance snapshots supplied the process-memory evidence. Worker level-3 BBAI logging recorded 12,089 irrigation-chain selections and 1,041 no-usable-route evaluations from turns 152 through 496. Every selected route had positive value and stayed within the 12-plot limit; 344 failed searches reached the exact depth-12 boundary, exercising the highest valid `(plot, steps)` state without an out-of-bounds error, assertion, crash or Python traceback. The largest search visited only 59 states. Despite exhaustive logging producing about 487 MB of BBAI output, SASGameRecord showed that the 32-bit process peaked at about 1.17 GB working set with about 1.88 GB of virtual address space still available, so the bounded state expansion showed no practical memory problem.

Found and investigated through the systematic AdvCiv-SAS archaeology with the help of ChatGPT-5.6-Sol; fixed and documented with the help of GPT-5.6-Sol thanks.

## KI#215 - (Fixed inherited K-Mod/Base AdvCiv bug) No-site Settler cleanup could unload unrelated transport cargo

When an AI Settler older than 20 turns has no reachable valid city site, inherited cleanup code first tried to remove it from its transport through `getTransportUnit()->unloadAll()`. That operation belongs to the transport and unloads every passenger that can disembark, so cleaning up one obsolete no-site Settler could also eject unrelated Settlers or military cargo.

The passenger-side `CvUnit::unload()` has exactly the required semantics. At sea or another invalid unloading location, `canUnload()` fails and this Settler remains aboard, preserving the existing `getTransportUnit() == NULL` gate that prevents it from being scrapped. At a valid unloading location, only this Settler detaches and the other cargo remains aboard.

The exact `unloadAll()` behavior is present at the earliest available K-Mod source boundary and survived through Base AdvCiv into AdvCiv-SAS. The fix replaces it with this Settler's `unload()` and retains every subsequent cleanup and mission check. No transport-group policy, pathfinding, RNG or ordinary unloading behavior changes.

Found through the systematic AdvCiv-SAS archaeology and investigated with the help of ChatGPT-5.6-Sol; fixed and documented with the help of GPT-5.6-Sol thanks.
